internalNote: Built from Kevin's own per-song extraction CSV (Original_Sacred_Harp_1971_cumulative_extraction.csv), 541 songs, pages 23-573. Gaps within that range (68 page numbers, e.g. 24-25, and scattered pages mostly in the 190s-560s) are real pages with nothing to extract - front matter, section dividers, or blank/illustration pages - not gaps in the extraction. 57 songs have no meter and 67 have no key recorded; this reflects real, printed variation in the book itself, not omissions in the transcription. Full book-level bibliographic facts (compiler, publisher, printer, meterAbbreviationKey, etc.) live on this edition's own record in tunebook-library.js, not duplicated here. No index cross-check has been done against this book's own printed index yet - this is a first-pass build from the extraction CSV alone.

23t.title: Canon
23t.firstLine: Welcome, welcome, ev'ry guest, Welcome to our music feast:

23b.title: Fire Alarm
23b.firstLine: Bells are ringing, What's the matter, See the smoke and hear the clatter,

26.title: Samaria
26.firstLine: My spirit looks to God alone,
26.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

27.title: Bethel
27.firstLine: O for a closer walk with God,
27.scriptureReference: “And Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.”—Gen. 5:24
27.historicalNote: William Cowper was born in 1731 and died in 1800. He was a co-worker with John Newton. Both Newton and Cowper were left motherless at an early age, Newton when he was seven, and Cowper when he was six. David R. Breed, D.D., in his work on the “History and Use of Hymns and Hymn Tunes,” contrasts the very different sufferings through which Newton and Cowper came to religion.

28t.title: Aylesbury
28t.scriptureReference: “According to thy name, O God, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth: thy right hand is full of righteousness. For this God is our God forever and ever; he will be our guide even unto death.”—Ps. 48:10, 14
28t.historicalNote: This tune appeared in many of the old song books, including works associated with William Billings, Southern Harmony (1835), Mason's Sacred Harp (1840), and Missouri Harmony (1837). The hymn is said to come from “The Beauty of the Church,” or “Gospel Worship and Order.” It has six stanzas. The note describes Aylesbury as an older minor tune and states that it was composed by James Green.

28b.title: Wells
28b.firstLine: Life is the time to serve the Lord,
28b.scriptureReference: “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.”—Eccl. 9:10

29t.title: Fairfield
29t.firstLine: Come, humble sinner, in whose breast A thousand thoughts revolve,
29t.scriptureReference: “And so I will go in unto the king, ... and if I perish, I perish. When the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favor in his sight; and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand.”—Esther 4:16; 5:2
29t.historicalNote: Fairfield is described as appearing in numerous early publications, including Southern Harmony, Temple Harp, Little & Smith's publications, and others. The note states that nothing is known of the author of the music despite the printed credit to Hitchcock.

29b.title: Tribulation
29b.firstLine: Death, 'tis a melancholy day To those who have no God,
29b.historicalNote: Chopin was born in 1810 and died in 1849. He was described as one of the great masters of music, followed by an account of remarks attributed to him near his death.

30t.title: Love Divine
30t.scriptureReference: “God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him.”—1 John 4:16
30t.historicalNote: The above tune was composed by Thomas Waller. He lived in Upson county, Ga.

30b.title: Prospect
30b.firstLine: Why should we start and fear to die?
30b.scriptureReference: “Blessed is the dead who die in the Lord.”—Rev. 14:13
30b.historicalNote: The original title to this hymn was “Christ's Presence Makes Death Easy.” The note identifies Prospect as one of the older melodies and says it appears in Southern Harmony, by Walker, page 92, in 1835, Christian Harmony, and many other books.

31t.title: Ninety-Third Psalm
31t.firstLine: Grace! 'tis a charming sound, Harmonious to the ear;
31t.historicalNote: The note discusses Philip Doddridge and Jeremiah Ingalls and traces the tune through Ingalls' song books, Southern Harmony, Christian Harmony, Missouri Harmony, and other publications.

31b.title: Webster
31b.firstLine: Come we who love the Lord, And let our joys be known:
31b.scriptureReference: “If a man love me, he will keep my words.”—John 14:23
31b.historicalNote: The tune appears in Southern Harmony (1835) and other earlier sacred tune books. Its original name is given as “Heavenly Joys on Earth,” appearing in Watts' Hymns of Spiritual Songs.

32t.title: Corinth
32t.firstLine: Jesus, and shall it ever be, A mortal man ashamed of thee?
32t.scriptureReference: “Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and my words, ... of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed.”—Mark 8:38
32t.historicalNote: The tune is credited to John Messengale, although the note expresses doubt that he wrote the music and suggests he may instead have made important changes. Earlier appearances include Missouri Harmony, Mason's Sacred Harp, and Hesperian Harp.

32b.title: Distress
32b.firstLine: So fades the lovely blooming flow'r, Frail, smiling solace of an hour;
32b.scriptureReference: “Then they cried unto the Lord in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses.”—Ps. 107:6

33t.title: Weeping Saviour
33t.firstLine: Did Christ o'er sinners weep? And shall our cheeks be dry?
33t.scriptureReference: And when he was come near, he beheld the city and wept over it.—Luke 19:41
33t.historicalNote: The note gives biographical information on Benjamin Beddome and states that Weeping Saviour is probably an English air found in early American tune books. Joseph Barnby is identified as author of the music.

33b.title: Abbeville
33b.firstLine: Come, Holy Spirit, come, With energy divine,
33b.scriptureReference: They were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.—Acts 4:31

34t.title: The Gospel Pool
34t.firstLine: Beside the gospel pool, Appointed for the poor,
34t.scriptureReference: “Expectation of the poor shall not perish forever.”—Ps. 9:18
34t.historicalNote: The note states that Gospel Pool was composed by the author for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp in 1869.

34b.title: The Teacher's Farewell
34b.firstLine: Our school now closes out, And we today must part;
34b.scriptureReference: “Deal truly; he is just, he shall surely live, saith the Lord God.”—Ezek. 18:9
34b.historicalNote: The tune was composed in 1858 but not published until 1869. The page identifies the poetry as original. The note says neither tune on page 34 had been found in any other book.

35.title: Saints Bound for Heaven
35.firstLine: Our bondage it shall end by and by, by and by,

musicAttribution.credit: E. J. King and Wm. Walker

35.scriptureReference: “I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the Land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.”—Deut. 5:6. “Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”—John 8:32
35.historicalNote: Described as an old melody appearing in Southern Harmony and later editions. The tune in this book is credited to King and Walker about 1834; the alto was added by S. M. Denson in 1911.

36t.title: America
36t.firstLine: My soul repeat his praise, Whose mercies are so great,
36t.scriptureReference: “The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy.”—Ps. 103:8

36b.title: Ninety-Fifth
36b.firstLine: When I can read my title clear, To mansions in the skies,
36b.scriptureReference: “Give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall.”—2 Pet. 1:10
36b.historicalNote: The original hymn title is given as “Hope of Heaven,” or “Supported Under Trials on Earth.” The tune is credited to Colton, about whom the editors state they could find nothing definite.

37t.title: Esther
37t.firstLine: Young ladies, all attention give, You that in wicked pleasures live;
37t.scriptureReference: “Flee, youthful lusts, call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”—2 Tim. 2:22
37t.historicalNote: J. S. Terry is described as a music teacher who composed four pieces in The Sacred Harp in 1869. The words were arranged by Terry to suit the tune.

37b.title: Liverpool
37b.firstLine: Young people all, attention give, And hear what I shall say;
37b.scriptureReference: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth.”—Eccl. 12:1
37b.historicalNote: The hymn was found in Mercer's Cluster, page 146, headed “Solemn Addresses to Young People.” The editors found no author or date for the hymn and considered it probably an English production. Liverpool is credited to M. C. H. Davis.

38t.title: Winter
38t.firstLine: His hoary frost, his fleecy snow, Descend and clothe the ground;
38t.scriptureReference: “And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter.”—John 10:22
38t.historicalNote: The note refers to the Daniel Read history under Windham and lists appearances of Winter in Southern Harmony, Missouri Harmony, and other song books.

38b.title: Windham
38b.firstLine: Broad is the road that leads to death And thousands walk together there;
38b.scriptureReference: “Wide is the gate, broad is the way that leadeth to destruction. Straight is the gate, narrow is the way that leadeth unto life.”—Matt. 7:13, 14
38b.historicalNote: Daniel Read is identified as the author of the music. The note discusses his American Song Book (1785), Columbia Harmony (1793), other collections, and his authorship of several standard tunes.

39t.title: Detroit
39t.firstLine: Do not I love Thee, O my Lord? Behold my heart, and see,
39t.scriptureReference: “He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest I love thee.”—John 21:15
39t.historicalNote: Biographical note on Philip Doddridge, identifying him as a Nonconformist minister, scholar, orator, theologian, and composer of standard hymns and sacred music.

39b.title: Sharpsburg
39b.firstLine: Blest Jesus while in mortal flesh I hold my frail abode;

musicAttribution.credit: J. P. Reese and J. A. T. Shell

39b.scriptureReference: “Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven.”—Ps. 33:1

40.title: Lenox
40.firstLine: Blow ye the trumpet blow, The gladly solemn sound;
40.scriptureReference: “Blow the trumpet tenth and seventh month”—Lev. 25:9
40.historicalNote: The original title of the hymn is given as “The Year of Jubilee.” It was published in the author's Hymn Book for 1750. The note rejects an attribution to Toplady and gives brief biographical information on Lewis Edson.

41.title: Home in Heaven
41.firstLine: A home in Heaven! What a joyful thought,

musicAttribution.credit: W. W. Parks & M. H. Thomas

41.historicalNote: W. W. Parks and M. H. Thomas prepared the tune for the second appendix to The Sacred Harp in 1859. The note traces appearances in Christian Harmony and Lute of Zion and states that no information was found identifying the author of the words.

42.title: Clamanda
42.firstLine: Say, now ye lovely social band, Who walk the way to Canaan's land;
42.scriptureReference: “If the Lord delight in us, then he will bring us into this land, and give it to us.”—Num. 14:8
42.historicalNote: The tune appeared on page 42 of The Sacred Harp in 1844. The editors state that they were unable to trace the history or words of the tune and describe it as a favorite among older singers.

43.title: Primrose Hill
43.firstLine: When I can read my title clear To mansions in the skies,
43.historicalNote: The original hymn title is given as “The Hopes of Heaven Our Support Under Trials on Earth.” The note says the text appeared in Watts's Hymns and Spiritual Songs; the tune is identified as “Marlow,” arranged by Dr. Lowell Mason, while the author of the music is stated to be unknown.

44.title: The Converted Thief
44.firstLine: As on the cross the Saviour hung, And wept, and bled, and died;
44.scriptureReference: “And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.”—Luke 23:42
44.historicalNote: The note says the words were taken from Mercer's Cluster, page 31, published in 1828 by Rev. Jesse Mercer, while also stating that the editors had been unable to obtain the author's name. The tune is described as longstanding and as appearing in Southern Harmony (1835) and earlier tune books.

45t.title: New Britain
45t.firstLine: Amazing grace! how sweet the sound, That saved a wretch like me!
45t.scriptureReference: “And David the king came and sat before the Lord, and said, Who am I, O Lord?”—1 Chron. 17:16. “According unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.”—Ps. 51:1
45t.historicalNote: The original title in Olney's Selections is given as “Faith's Review and Expectation.” The note provides biographical information on John Newton and identifies him as the author of “Amazing grace.”

45b.title: Imandra
45b.firstLine: Farewell, my dear brethren, the time is at hand,
45b.scriptureReference: “He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.”—John 3:14
45b.historicalNote: The heading cites “Dover Selection,” page 196. The note below the tune instead states that it is taken from “Dover's Selections,” page 192. The tune also appeared in Southern Harmony, page 34, 1835, and Sacred Harp, 1844–1869. None of the hymn books consulted identified the author of the words.

46.title: Let Us Sing
46.firstLine: Shall we ever meet again at the house, at the house,
46.scriptureReference: Meet in “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.”—2 Cor. 5:1
46.historicalNote: The note identifies W. F. Moore as the first president of the Tallapoosa Singing Convention and states that he composed several songs in The Sacred Harp. This song is described as partly the old melody “Let Us Walk in the Light of God.”

47t.title: Primrose
47t.firstLine: Salvation, O the joyful sound, 'Tis pleasure to our ears;
47t.historicalNote: The text first appeared in Watts's Hymns and Spiritual Songs under the title “Salvation.” The note discusses later textual changes and traces the tune through Southern Harmony, Missouri Harmony, and other books.

47b.title: Idumea
47b.firstLine: And am I born to die? To lay this body down!
47b.scriptureReference: “A time to be born and a time to die.”—Eccl. 3:2

48t.title: Devotion
48t.firstLine: Sweet is the day of sacred rest; No mortal cares shall seize my breast;
48t.scriptureReference: “To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night, upon an instrument of ten strings, and upon a psaltery; upon the harp with a solemn sound.”—Ps. 92:2, 3
48t.historicalNote: The note explains that the words as arranged begin with the second verse of the original hymn. Amarick Hall is identified as author of the music, and Devotion is said to have been first published by Hall in 1811.

48b.title: Kedron
48b.firstLine: Thou Man of grief, remember me, Thou never canst thyself forget,

49t.title: Old Hundred
49t.firstLine: O come, loud anthems let us sing, Loud thanks to our Almighty King.
49t.scriptureReference: “Sing, O ye heavens, ... shout, ye lower parts of the earth: break forth into singing, ye mountains, O forest, and every tree therein.”—Isa. 44:23
49t.historicalNote: The note gives biographical information on Bishop Ken. Authorship of the music is discussed as disputed: some attribute Old Hundred to Luther, others to Bourgeois, while the editors say it is generally conceded to William the Frenchman.

49b.title: Mear
49b.firstLine: Will God forever cast us off? His wrath forever smoke Against the people of His love,
49b.scriptureReference: “What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much long-suffering.”—Rom. 9:22
49b.historicalNote: The note describes two competing claims for authorship. One credits Aaron Williams; another American claim places an earlier form of the tune in 1726 but does not name its composer.

50.title: Jordan's Shore
50.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand, And cast a wishful eye,
50.scriptureReference: “Thine eyes shall see the King in His beauty: behold the land that is very far.”—Isa. 33:17
50.historicalNote: The page states that the tune as printed here was re-arranged by Geo. B. Daniel in 1911.

51.title: My Home
51.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand, And cast a wishful eye
51.historicalNote: Biographical note on Samuel Stennett. Nothing is known of C. F. Letson, the person credited with the tune, and the editors state that no trace could be found of when he composed it.

52t.title: Albion
52t.firstLine: Come, ye that love the Lord, And let your joys be known;
52t.scriptureReference: “When two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”—Matt. 18:20
52t.historicalNote: The tune is credited in Southern Harmony, 1835, to Mr. Boyd and also appears in Missouri Harmony, 1837, and earlier collections. The editors were unable to obtain biographical information about Boyd or determine the date of composition.

52b.title: Charlestown
52b.firstLine: “Mercy, O Thou Son of David,” Thus blind Bartimeus prayed,
52b.scriptureReference: “Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me. And many charged him that he should hold his peace.”—Mark 10:47, 48
52b.historicalNote: Stephen Jenks of New Canaan, Connecticut, published Delights of Harmony in 1805; the note states that twenty-six tunes in that book were composed by him.

53.title: Jerusalem
53.firstLine: Jesus, my all to heav'n is gone, He whom I fix my hopes upon;
53.scriptureReference: “Hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began.”—Titus 1:2
53.historicalNote: The original title of the hymn was “Christ, the Sinner's Way to God.” Biographical information on John Cennick follows. The tune is printed as arranged by Wm. Walker about 1832.

54.title: The Blessed Lamb
54.firstLine: See the happy spirits waiting On the banks beyond the stream;
54.scriptureReference: “Make sweet Melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered.”—Isa. 23:16
54.historicalNote: The tune was first published in The Sacred Harp by B. F. White in 1869. The editors could not locate it in an earlier book or identify its author, and note that its words look toward the afterlife.

55.title: Sister's Farewell
55.firstLine: Farewell, dear brothers, fare you well, Pray do not weep for me,
55.scriptureReference: “Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven. For in the resurrection they ... are as the angels of God in heaven.”—Matt. 19:14; 22:30
55.historicalNote: Prof. A. J. McLendon is identified as author of both tune and words, written in memory of Bertha B. Brantly, youngest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. D. Laminack. Professor McLendon was residing in Carroll County, Georgia, at the time of the 1909 note.

56t.title: Columbiana
56t.firstLine: May the grace of Christ our Saviour, And the Father's boundless love,
56t.scriptureReference: “And God is able to make all grace abound toward you.”—2 Cor. 8:9
56t.historicalNote: The words also appear in Mercer's Cluster, page 335. The note gives biographical information on D. P. White, a son of B. F. White, and identifies several of his Sacred Harp compositions.

56b.title: Villulia
56b.firstLine: Mercy O thou Son of David, Thus poor blind Bartimeus pray'd,
56b.scriptureReference: “Because of the blindness of their heart.”—Eph. 4:18

57.title: Christian Soldier
57.firstLine: Am I a soldier of the cross, A foll'wr of the Lamb?
57.scriptureReference: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.”—1 Cor. 16:13
57.historicalNote: The hymn was first entitled “Holy Fortitude.” The note states that it was published after Watts preached from 1 Corinthians 16:13 in 1709 and that the tune appeared in William Walker's Southern Harmony, page 45, 1835.

58.title: Pisgah
58.firstLine: Jesus, Thou art the sinner's friend, As such I look to Thee,
58.historicalNote: The hymn was first published in Burnham's new hymn book. J. C. Lowry is described as a musician of standing who wrote a great deal of sacred music; the editors could not ascertain his birth or death dates.

59.title: Holy Manna
59.firstLine: Brethren, we have met to worship, And adore the Lord our God;
59.scriptureReference: “Worship the Lord in beauty of holiness.”—Ps. 29:2. “It is manna. This is the bread which the Lord hath given you to eat.”—Ex. 16:15
59.historicalNote: Described as a longstanding convention and singing-society tune. The editors credit J. W. Moore with the music. The note also mentions Moore's Encyclopedia of Music and appearances in Southern Harmony and Songs for the Army.

60.title: Days of Worship
60.firstLine: Dear people we have met today, To sing, to hear, to preach and pray;

musicAttribution.credit: B. F. and E. K. Davis

60.scriptureReference: “When ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation.”—Cor.—14:26

61.title: Sweet Rivers
61.firstLine: Sweet rivers of redeeming love Lie just before mine eye,
61.historicalNote: The tune appears in Southern Harmony (Walker, 1835), p. 166, where it is credited to Moore. The note says it was taken from Baptist Harmony, p. 68, and considers J. W. Moore of Vermont the probable composer; it was published in an Encyclopedia of Music in 1854 and an edition was added in 1876.

62.title: Parting Hand
62.firstLine: My Christian friends, in bonds of love, Whose hearts in sweetest union join,
62.historicalNote: Jeremiah Ingalls (1764–1828), a Massachusetts native, published Christian Harmony in 1804. The note says Parting Hand was composed in 1803 and suggests Ingalls may have written its words as well as the music; it also points to Northfield for a fuller biographical sketch.

63.title: Coronation
63.firstLine: All hail the pow'r of Jesus' name! Let angels prostrate fall,
63.historicalNote: See history of Oliver Holden on page 313.

64.title: Nashville
64.firstLine: The Lord into His garden come, The spices yield their rich perfumes,
64.historicalNote: The note says the tune was originally called Garden Hymn and is sometimes credited to William Campbell, author of several other hymns named there. The printed credit line gives Jeremiah Ingalls, 1800; Campbell, translator, 1804; and Alexander Johnson (?) on the music side.

65.title: Sweet Prospect
65.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand, And cast a wishful eye,
65.historicalNote: The note identifies Samuel Stennett as a Doctor of Divinity and author of the popular hymn On Jordan's Stormy Banks I Stand; he died in 1795. William Walker composed the tune and died in Spartanburg, South Carolina.

66.title: Home
66.firstLine: While trav'ling through this vale of tears, Amidst temptations, doubts and fears;
66.historicalNote: The heading identifies the piece as original and credits both music and poetry to B. F. White, 1869, for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp. The chorus changes from A Minor to A Major.

67.title: Columbus
67.firstLine: Oh, once I had a glorious view Of my redeeming Lord,
67.historicalNote: The words were selected from Mercer's Cluster by Jesse Mercer of Powellton, Georgia, 1823; the hymn there was titled Perplexed, But Not In Despair. The note says the author of the tune Columbus is unknown and that William Walker published it in Southern Harmony (1835), p. 55.

68t.title: Salem
68t.firstLine: He dies, the Friend of sinners dies! Lo Salem's daughters weep around:
68t.historicalNote: No examined source identifies the tune's author. The note cites Missouri Harmony (Carden, 1827 and 1837), p. 47, and Southern Harmony (Walker, 1837 and 1848), p. 53; it states that the full hymn has six verses.

68b.title: Ortonville
68b.firstLine: How sweet the name of Jesus sounds, In a believer's ear,

harmonizationAttribution.credit: B. F. White; S. M. Denson

68b.historicalNote: The heading says the tune was rearranged by B. F. White in 1858 and that the alto is by S. M. Denson.

69t.title: Minister's Farewell
69t.firstLine: Dear friends, farewell! I do you tell, Since you and I must part;

69b.title: Farewell to All
69b.firstLine: And now my friends, both old and young, I hope in Christ you'll still go on;
69b.historicalNote: The heading gives J. P. R., 1852 on the text side, J. P. Reese, 1852 on the music side, and alto by S. M. Denson, 1911.

70t.title: Gainsville
70t.firstLine: Lord, we come before Thee now, At Thy feet we humbly bow;
70t.historicalNote: The heading marks the tune Original. The note identifies W. D. Jones, usually called Wills Jones, of Carroll County, Georgia, as composer and says the hymn text was taken from Mercer's Cluster, published in 1823.

70b.title: Save, Mighty Lord
70b.firstLine: Jesus, my all, to heav'n is gone, Save, mighty Lord,

musicAttribution.credit: J. A. and J. F. Wade

70b.historicalNote: The heading says the tune was re-arranged by J. S. J. in 1909. The note says John Cennick published the words in 1743; the song's name had been changed from O Save to Save, Mighty Lord; and J. A. and J. F. Wade lived in South Carolina when they composed the music.

71.title: Leander
71.firstLine: My soul forsakes her vain delight, And bids the world farewell;
71.historicalNote: The note describes Leander as a very old tune and says it appears in Southern Harmony (Walker, 1835), p. 128, where it is credited to Austin; it also cites Missouri Harmony (1837), p. 120. No information concerning Austin was found.

72t.title: The Weary Soul
72t.firstLine: Ye weary, heavy laden souls, Who are oppressed and sore,
72t.historicalNote: J. T. White, nephew of B. F. White, is identified as author of the tune. The words are taken from Zion's Songster, p. 185, seventh edition, 1832.

72b.title: Bellevue
72b.firstLine: How firm a foundation, ye saints of the Lord,
72b.historicalNote: The page states that in The Sacred Harp this tune is credited to Z. Chambers.

73t.title: Cusseta
73t.firstLine: Show pity, Lord; O Lord, forgive; Let a repenting rebel live:
73t.historicalNote: The note says Prof. John Massengale wrote the melody sometime between 1840 and 1844 and composed many Sacred Harp songs.

73b.title: Arlington
73b.firstLine: I'm not ashamed to own my Lord Or to defend His cause;
73b.historicalNote: The note identifies Dr. Thomas Augustine Arne as composer of Arlington and gives biographical information about the English composer.

74t.title: The Enquirer
74t.firstLine: I'm not ashamed to own my Lord, Or to defend His cause,
74t.historicalNote: The note calls this one of Major B. F. White's original tunes, composed for the early editions of The Sacred Harp. The words are by Isaac Watts.

74b.title: King of Peace
74b.firstLine: Lord, I cannot let Thee go, Till a blessing Thou bestow:

75.title: I Would See Jesus
75.firstLine: I would see Jesus when the flow'rs Of joy adorn my way;
75.historicalNote: The note says this is an original song composed especially for The Sacred Harp by Prof. Breedlove and supposes him to be author of the words as well as the music. It also states that the last two verses are taken from Horatio Bonner's Hymn of Faith (1858).

76t.title: Holiness
76t.firstLine: Daniel's wisdom may I know, John's divine communion feel;
76t.historicalNote: The note says the words are taken from Zion Songster, 1832, p. 288, seventh edition.

76b.title: Desire for Piety
76b.firstLine: 'Tis my desire with God to walk, Till the warfare is over, hallelujah,
76b.historicalNote: The heading cites Baptist Harmony, p. 479, while the prose note says the words are selected from Baptist Harmony, p. 457. The prose page reference is retained in sourcePage and the discrepancy is noted here.

77t.title: The Child of Grace
77t.firstLine: How happy's every child of grace, Who feels his sins forgiven;
77t.historicalNote: The note calls this one of Charles Wesley's best hymns, first published in 1759, and says John Wesley considered it one of his brother's best hymns.

77b.title: Talbotton
77b.firstLine: Hark! my soul, it is the Lord; 'Tis the Saviour, hear His word!

78.title: Stafford
78.firstLine: See what a living stone The builders did refuse,
78.historicalNote: The note identifies Daniel Read as author of the tune and mentions several other tunes by him in Columbian Harmony (1793).

79.title: The Old Ship of Zion
79.firstLine: What ship is this that will take us all home, O glory hallelujah,
79.historicalNote: The note traces the hymn 'Voices Crying Out in the Wilderness' as far back as The American Vocalist, says the names of both hymn and tune authors have been lost, and notes that in the old Sacred Harp the tune is credited to Thomas W. Carter.

80t.title: Shouting Song
80t.firstLine: Jesus, grant us all a blessing, Shouting, singing, send it down;
80t.historicalNote: The note says the words are from Zion Songster, p. 268 (1832), with no author given. Major White remodeled an older outline into practically a new tune about 1844 and added the chorus.

80b.title: Service of the Lord
80b.firstLine: Farewell, vain world, I'm going home; I am bound to die in the army,

81t.title: Beach Spring
81t.firstLine: Come, ye sinners, poor and needy, Weak and wounded, sick and sore,
81t.historicalNote: The note identifies Joseph Hart (1712–1768) as author of the hymn and says this is an old melody for which the examined books give neither date nor author.

81b.title: Cookham
81b.firstLine: Hark! the herald angels sing, “Glory to the new-born King;
81b.historicalNote: The heading cites Psalmist, hymn 207. The note says Cookham is among the oldest American tunes, selected from Baptist Harmony, p. 327, and refers also to Southern Harmony (1835), p. 8.

82t.title: Bound for Canaan
82t.firstLine: O when shall I see Jesus, And reign with Him above,
82t.historicalNote: The note says the original name was Evening Song and gives biographical information about Rev. John Leland. It adds that E. J. King made material changes in the tune and rearranged it about 1844.

82b.title: Edgefield
82b.firstLine: How tedious and tasteless the hours When Jesus no longer I see!

83t.title: Vale of Sorrow
83t.firstLine: While in this vale of sorrow I travel on in pain;
83t.historicalNote: The page states only 'Published in 1769' and does not identify the author or composer.

83b.title: The Dying Minister
83b.firstLine: The time is swiftly rolling on, When I must faint and die;
83b.historicalNote: The note says Elder E. Dumas composed the tune in 1854, was a Georgia Primitive Baptist minister, composed sixteen tunes in the book, served as a reviser in 1869, and died in 1884.

84.title: Amsterdam
84.firstLine: Rise, my soul, and stretch thy wings, Thy better portion trace,
84.historicalNote: The note gives biographical information about Rev. Robert Seagraves and James Nares and calls Amsterdam one of the great old melodies.

85.title: The Morning Trumpet
85.firstLine: O when shall I see Jesus, And reign with Him above,
85.historicalNote: The note states that John Leland was born in Massachusetts in 1754 and died in 1844.

86.title: Little Children
86.firstLine: Come, little children, now we may Partake a little morsel,
86.historicalNote: The note says the words as well as the music are supposed to have been composed by T. W. Carter.

87.title: Sweet Canaan
87.firstLine: O who will come and go with me? I am bound for the land of Canaan;
87.historicalNote: The note says the original name was O Canaan, Bright Canaan and discusses older verses and John Wesley's attempted alteration.

88t.title: Done with the World
88t.firstLine: Jesus, my all, to heaven is gone, And I don't expect to stay much longer here;
88t.historicalNote: The printed heading gives John Cennick, 1843. The prose note instead says the hymn was written by Cennick and found in his Sacred Hymns, 1743, under the title Following Christ, the Sinner's Way to God. The conflict is preserved rather than normalized.

88b.title: Mount Zion
88b.firstLine: O for a thousand tongues to sing My great Redeemer's praise,

89.title: The Church's Desolation
89.firstLine: Well may thy servants mourn, my God, The Church's desolation;
89.historicalNote: The note says the editors were unable to find the author of the words; early song books likewise gave neither hymn author nor date of composition.

90.title: Look Out
90.firstLine: My brethren all, on you I call, Arise and look around you;
90.historicalNote: The note says Major B. F. White composed both music and words. The tune has been printed regularly in The Sacred Harp since the 1844 edition and stands much as it did when first composed.

91.title: Assurance
91.firstLine: Now shall my soul be lifted high, be lifted high, Above my foes around,
91.historicalNote: The words in the piece are taken from Revelation 14:13. William Billings was born in Boston in 1746 and died in 1800.

92.title: Burk
92.firstLine: The glorious light of Zion Is spreading far and wide
92.historicalNote: The tune appeared in the first Sacred Harp in 1844 and remained practically the same through later revisions. The note says B. F. White either composed the words and chorus or altered them so substantially that no trace of them can be found except in books printed after his tune.

93.title: Frozen Heart
93.firstLine: Lord, shed a beam of heavenly day, To melt this stubborn stone away;
93.historicalNote: See the history of Joseph Hart under Beach Spring, page 81. The note states that the music was re-arranged by Prof. King in 1844 for The Sacred Harp.

94.title: Never Part
94.firstLine: Come humble sinner in whose breast A thousand thoughts revolve,
94.historicalNote: The tune continues onto page 95. The note says little is known of John Carroll, author of Never Part.

95.title: Vernon
95.firstLine: Come, O Thou traveler unknown, Whom still I hold, but cannot see;
95.historicalNote: Vernon is described as one of the oldest melodies, with its composition dating to the first part of the nineteenth century; the note refers to Southern Harmony by Walker.

96.title: Happy Matches
96.firstLine: When Thou, my righteous Judge, shall come To take Thy ransomed people home, Shall I among them stand?

musicAttribution.credit: B. F. White and E. J. King

96.historicalNote: The note gives a biographical sketch of Lady Huntingdon (Selina Shirley), describing her support of the Methodists and her association with George Whitefield.

97.title: We'll Soon Be There
97.firstLine: Oh, who will come and go with me, We'll shout and sing Hosanna,
97.historicalNote: The heading credits the tune to Oliver Bradfield and the alto to J. P. Reese, 1859.

98.title: Dull Care
98.firstLine: Why should we at our lot complain, Or grieve at our distress?
98.historicalNote: The note says the editors were unable to find the author of the words in the hymnals available to them, though the text may occur in earlier hymn books.

99.title: Gospel Trumpet
99.firstLine: Hark! how the gospel trumpet sounds! Thro' all the world the echo bounds;
99.historicalNote: The hymn was selected from Mercer's Cluster, page 409, by Jesse Mercer of Powellton, Georgia, revised 1830. The note calls it an old hymn and says the author's name is not given in the hymn books, despite the printed left-side credit to Charles Cole.

100.title: The Bower of Prayer
100.firstLine: To leave my dear friends, and with neighbors to part, And go from my home it afflicts not my heart,
100.historicalNote: The page says the tune was re-arranged by E. J. King. The note states that it was said to have been originally arranged from a flute interlude in one of Haydn's themes; when compiling The Sacred Harp, King made slight changes in the words and notes, but not enough to receive credit for the tune.

101t.title: Canaan's Land
101t.firstLine: O for a breeze of heav'nly love To waft my soul away
101t.historicalNote: The heading says E. J. King applied the words in 1859. The note says Amariah Hall was born in Massachusetts in 1785, was a farmer, manufacturer, hotel keeper, and singing-school teacher, and composed a number of tunes.

101b.title: Holy City
101b.firstLine: There is a holy city, A happy world above,

102.title: Fulfillment
102.firstLine: See how the Scriptures are fulfilling, Poor sinners are returning home,
102.historicalNote: The words are taken from Zion Songster, page 120, by Thomas Mason, published in 1832, seventh edition. The note says Prof. King arranged the tune for The Sacred Harp and that none of the hymn books consulted gives the name of the hymn's author.

103.title: Animation
103.firstLine: And let this feeble body fail, And let it faint or die;
103.historicalNote: The hymn was published in the second series of Charles Wesley's Funeral Hymns and originally had nine stanzas. The note calls Animation a very old tune, printed early in Southern Harmony (Walker, 1835), page 58, and says no trace can be found of the author of the music.

104.title: The Lovely Story
104.firstLine: A story most lovely I'll tell, Of Jesus O wondrous surprise,
104.historicalNote: The note says it is not known whether Prof. E. J. King composed or re-arranged the words. It describes him as a fine singer and teacher who wrote acceptable hymns and tunes.

105.title: Jewett
105.firstLine: Amazing grace how sweet the sound! That saved a wretch like me!

106.title: Ecstasy
106.firstLine: Oh when shall I see Jesus, And reign with him above?
106.historicalNote: The note says the original hymn was written by Rev. John Leland, born in 1754 and died in 1844. It states that Ecstasy is supposed to have been composed by Prof. Thomas W. Carter sometime before the first revision of The Sacred Harp in 1845.

107.title: Russia
107.firstLine: My spirit looks to God alone, My rock and refuge is His throne.
107.historicalNote: The note says the tune was formerly on page 274 of The Sacred Harp, was removed and replaced by Golden Harp and Baldwin, and was first published in Daniel Read's Columbian Harmony in 1793.

108t.title: Weeping Sinners
108t.firstLine: Weeping sinners, dry your tears, Jesus on the throne appears;
108t.historicalNote: The heading marks the tune Original. The note says the hymn is in none of the books examined and suggests that if Rees did not compose the words, he changed them so substantially that their identity was lost.

108b.title: The Traveler
108b.firstLine: Trav'ler haste, the night comes on, Many a shining hour is gone;
108b.historicalNote: The heading says Arr. by A. Ogletree, 1868. See sketch of Prof. A. Ogletree under Heavenly Dove, page 371.

109.title: Carnsville
109.firstLine: I love my blessed Saviour, I feel I'm in his favor,
109.historicalNote: The words are taken from Zion Songster, revised edition of 1830, page 78.

110.title: Mount Vernon
110.firstLine: What solemn sound the ear invades, What wraps the land in sorrow's shade?
110.historicalNote: The note calls Mount Vernon an old tune dating back to the days of Billings, Law, and Holden, cites Southern Harmony (Walker, 1835), page 52, and says none of the books consulted gives the author's name.

111t.title: Journey Home
111t.firstLine: Oh, who will come and go with me, I'm on my journey home,
111t.historicalNote: The heading marks the tune Original and prints John Moffitt at the left. The prose note, however, says the words are from Watts' Hymns and Spiritual Songs, where the hymn is entitled Christ's Presence Makes Death Easy. The conflicting text attribution is preserved rather than reconciled.

111b.title: To Die No More
111b.firstLine: Why should we start, and fear to die? What timorous worms we mortals are,
111b.historicalNote: The note says Elder E. Dumas, author of the tune, assisted B. F. White in the revision of The Sacred Harp in 1869.

112.title: The Last Words of Copernicus
112.firstLine: Ye golden lamps of Heav'n, farewell, With all your feeble light;
112.historicalNote: The heading marks the tune Original. The note says Miss Sarah Lancaster was about ninety years old, living somewhere in Texas, and that the hymn is based on Revelation 22:5.

113.title: The Prodigal Son
113.firstLine: Afflictions, tho' they seem severe, Are oft in mercy sent:
113.historicalNote: The words appear in Zion Songster (Thomas Mason, 1832), page 21, Baptist Harmony, page 227, and Southern Harmony (Walker), page 70. The note says Prof. King re-arranged the tune for The Sacred Harp in 1844 and that the referenced books do not name the author of the words, despite the printed John Newton credit.

114.title: Saints Delight
114.firstLine: When I can read my title clear to mansions in the skies,
114.historicalNote: The note gives the original hymn title as The Hope's Of Heaven Our Support Under Trials on Earth and comments on wording differences in later verses.

115.title: Edmonds
115.firstLine: When Adam was created, He dwelt in Eden's shade;
115.historicalNote: The heading marks the tune Original.

116.title: Union
116.firstLine: Come, brothers and sisters who love one another, And have done for years that are gone;
116.historicalNote: The note says the hymn is from a very old edition, 1820, and was not found in any of the hymn books examined since that date.

117.title: Timmons
117.firstLine: Lord, thou wilt hear me when I pray; I am forever thine,
117.historicalNote: The tune was put in The Sacred Harp in place of Jordan's Shore in 1859. The prose note says no data could be found about E. T. Williams, while the heading reads E. F. Williams. It also cites L. Loyd's Hymn Book, page 441, and Mercer's Cluster, page 385, editions of 1823 and 1830.

118.title: Stockwood
118.firstLine: Sister, thou wast mild and lovely, Gentle as the summer breeze,
118.historicalNote: The heading marks the tune Original. The note says the hymn was composed on the death of a young lady, probably between 1830 and 1840. Stockwood was inserted in place of Ball Hill Removed. M. Mark Wynn is described as a noted teacher of music who wrote several tunes.

119.title: Heaven's My Home
119.firstLine: Come, all my dear brethren and help me to sing;

textAttribution.credit: R. H. Davis and J. S. Terry

musicAttribution.credit: Dr. R. H. Davis and J. S. Terry

119.historicalNote: The tune is supposed to have been composed about 1869 and is credited to R. H. Davis and J. S. Terry. The note says little is known of either man beyond their prominence in sacred musical conventions and societies from 1859 into the early seventies.

120.title: Chambers
120.firstLine: The Lord Jehovah reigns, And royal state maintains: His head with awful glories crowned.

harmonizationAttribution.credit: B. F. White; S. M. Denson

120.historicalNote: The heading says Arr. by B. F. White, 1869, with alto by S. M. Denson, 1911. The note says the tune replaced Lumpkin in 1869, the words were also re-arranged by White, and the present alto is believed to improve the tune.

121.title: Florence
121.firstLine: Not many years their rounds shall roll, Each moment brings it nigh;
121.scriptureReference: “The harvest is the end of the world.”—Matt. 13:39

122.title: All Is Well
122.firstLine: What's this that steals, that steals upon my frame?
122.scriptureReference: “Through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.”—2 Peter 1:1

123t.title: The Dying Christian
123t.firstLine: Ye objects of sense, and enjoyments of time, Which oft have delighted my heart,
123t.historicalNote: The Dying Christian is described as an old melody, much older than the 1844 Sacred Harp. E. J. King made valuable improvements to it in 1844.

123b.title: Cross of Christ
123b.firstLine: The cross of Christ inspires my heart To sing redeeming grace;

124.title: Lover of the Lord
124.firstLine: Lovers of pleasure more than God, For you He suffered pain;
124.historicalNote: Verses arranged in 1869. The tune was rearranged by R. H. Reeves in 1869 for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp. The printed historical note continues, “Its outlines were taken from the tune,” without completing that identification on this page.

125.title: Expression
125.firstLine: Oh, Jesus, my Saviour, I know thou art mine;
125.scriptureReference: “Then he shall reward every man according to his works.”—Matt. 16:27
125.historicalNote: The words were taken from Thomas B. Mason's Zion Songster, published in 1832, Seventh Edition. The editors could find no author for the tune; it is described as an old melody, and none of the books consulted identified the author of either music or words.

126.title: Babel's Streams
126.firstLine: By Babel's streams we sat and wept, While Zion we thought on;
126.scriptureReference: “We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof.”—Ps. 137:2
126.historicalNote: Described as one of the oldest melodies. Its music and words are strongly claimed to derive from Welsh musicians, and versions appear in works by Billings, Holden, Hall, Ingalls, and others, as well as Southern Harmony. The editors say it is believed the words concern the captivity of the Children of Israel at Babylon.

127.title: Greenfield
127.firstLine: How tedious and tasteless the hours, When Jesus no longer I see!
127.scriptureReference: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth I desire beside thee.”—Psa. 73:25
127.historicalNote: The hymn, titled “Delights in Christ,” was taken from Olney Hymns in 1779. The note gives brief biographical information on John Newton.

128.title: The Promised Land
128.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand, And cast a wistful eye
128.scriptureReference: “Thine eyes shall behold the King in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off.”—Isa. 33:17
128.historicalNote: The tune is credited in The Sacred Harp to Miss M. Durham. The editors could find no information about her or determine whether she arranged and altered the tune specifically for The Sacred Harp. Its melody and principal features are said to be traceable for more than a century; Southern Harmony, 1835, page 51, is cited for comparison.

129.title: Heavenly Armor
129.firstLine: And if you meet with troubles And trials on the way,
129.scriptureReference: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.”—John 14:27
129.historicalNote: The note states that William Walker composed the tune in 1828 and cites Southern Harmony, 1835, page 93, its 1849 edition, and Christian Harmony, 1867, revised 1901, page 238.

130.title: Millennium
130.firstLine: The time is soon coming, by the prophets foretold, When Zion in purity, the world shall behold.
130.scriptureReference: “But the end shall not be yet.”—Matt. 24:6
130.historicalNote: The note states that the tune was composed by William Walker in 1831 and refers to Southern Harmony.

131t.title: Messiah
131t.firstLine: He comes, he comes! to judge the world, A-loud th'archangel cries;
131t.historicalNote: The heading prints the music credit as “Carrol.” The note says William Walker credited the tune to “Carroll” in Christian Harmony, page 152, and Southern Harmony, 1835, page 97. The words and music are described as longstanding; some claimed the tune was taken from the oratorio Messiah. One additional verse was added in 1911.

131b.title: Invocation
131b.firstLine: Rise, my soul, and stretch thy wings, Thy better portion trace,
131b.historicalNote: The note states that the tune was printed in Southern Harmony by William Walker in 1835, page 72, and again in the 1840 edition on the same page.

132.title: Sinners Friend
132.firstLine: He dies! the friend of sinners dies! And He died on the cross for sinners,
132.scriptureReference: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.”—1 Tim. 1:15
132.historicalNote: The page says Isaac Watts's words were rearranged by J. P. R. in 1869 and that the music was arranged for the organ by J. P. Reese in 1869. The note identifies Reese as a Georgia musician and hymn writer with 35 compositions credited to him in The Sacred Harp.

133.title: Hebrew Children
133.firstLine: Where are the Hebrew children? Where are the Hebrew children? Where are the Hebrew children? Safe in the promised land.
133.scriptureReference: “These men were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.”—Dan. 3:21
133.historicalNote: The original name is given as “Where Now Are the Hebrew Children.” Peter Cartwright is described as a minister who used the tune in camp meetings; the tune is called one of the old American melodies and was first published in The Sacred Harp in 1844. The heading dates the credit “between 1820-1875,” while the biographical note states Cartwright died in 1872.

134.title: The Christian's Hope
134.firstLine: A few more days on earth to spend, And all my toils and cares shall end,
134.scriptureReference: “For we are saved by hope; but hope that is seen is no hope.”—Rom. 8:24
134.historicalNote: The tune is described as one of William Walker's compositions for Southern Harmony and is cited there in the 1835 and 1840 editions, page 74, and in Christian Harmony, page 327. The words were originally taken from Dover's Selections, page 173; their author could not be found.

135.title: Olney
135.firstLine: Come, thou Fount of ev'ry blessing, Tune my heart to sing thy grace;
135.scriptureReference: “The fountain is Christ.”—Zek. 13:1. “We shall receive the blessings from the Lord, and righteousness from the God of his salvation.”—Ps. 24:5
135.historicalNote: Biographical note on Robert Robinson: born in Norfolk, England, in 1735; converted under Whitefield; later associated successively with the Methodist, Baptist, Independent, and Unitarian traditions; died in 1790.

136.title: Morality
136.firstLine: While beauty and youth are in their full prime, And folly and fashion affect our whole time;
136.scriptureReference: “But I thy servant fear the Lord from my youth.”—2 Kings 18:12
136.historicalNote: Described as an old tune older than the oldest Southern books. It appears with the same words in Southern Harmony, 1835, page 44, and Missouri Harmony, 1827 and 1837, page 54. The note says the complete hymn contains six verses, but no consulted book identifies the author of either words or music.

137.title: Liberty
137.firstLine: No more beneath th'oppressive hand Of tyranny we groan.
137.scriptureReference: “Deliver me from the oppression of man.”—Ps. 119:134
137.historicalNote: Stephen Jenks published Delights of Harmony in 1805; twenty-six tunes in that book were composed by him. The note says he was a prolific composer and supposes that he also composed the words of Liberty.

138t.title: Adoration
138t.firstLine: Lord, when my raptured thought surveys creation's beauties o'er,
138t.scriptureReference: “Praise him for his mighty acts.”—150 Ps. 2

138b.title: Ogletree
138b.firstLine: Frequent the day of God returns To shed its quick'ning beams;
138b.historicalNote: The note states that S. M. Brown composed the tune and named it Ogletree in honor of Absalom Ogletree, who died in 1910.

139.title: Elysian
139.firstLine: Burst, ye emerald gates, and bring Round my raptured vision,
139.scriptureReference: “There was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.”—Rev. 4:3

140.title: Sweet Solitude
140.firstLine: Hail, solitude, thou gentle queen, Of modest air and brow serene!
140.scriptureReference: “The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them: and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.”—Isa. 35:1
140.historicalNote: The editors say little is known of Sweet Solitude. The earliest printing they could find was Southern Harmony, 1835, page 155. No consulted book identified the author of the words or music, and the tune was thought considerably older than 1835. It subsequently appeared in revisions of The Sacred Harp, with the alto added by S. M. Denson in 1911.

141.title: Complainer
141.firstLine: I am a great complainer, that bears the name of Christ;
141.scriptureReference: “These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts.”—Judge 16
141.historicalNote: The tune was composed by William Walker of Spartanburg, S.C., about 1835 for Southern Harmony.

142.title: Stratfield
142.firstLine: Through ev'ry age, eternal God, Thou art our rest, our safe abode;
142.scriptureReference: “Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool, what house will ye build me? saith the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?”—Act 7:49
142.historicalNote: Stratfield is described as one of the old-time minor melodies. It appeared in Missouri Harmony, 1837 and 1827, page 94, and was believed to be an English tune or one composed during the early settlement of America. The editors could not identify the author of the music. The hymn title is given as “God's Eternity and Man's Frailty.”

143.title: Plevel's Hymn
143.firstLine: While thee I seek, protecting Pow'r, Be my vain wishes stilled,
143.scriptureReference: “Power belongeth unto God; also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy; for thou renderest to every man according to his work.”—Ps. 62:11, 12
143.historicalNote: The note gives biographical information on Helen Maria Williams and Ignaz Joseph Pleyel. Williams is said to have composed the hymn while imprisoned; Pleyel was born in 1757 and died in Paris in 1831.

144.title: Jubilee
144.firstLine: Hark! the jubilee is sounding, O the joyful news is come;
144.scriptureReference: “For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men.”—Titus 2:11
144.historicalNote: Jubilee appeared in each edition of The Sacred Harp from 1844 to 1869 and in several other tunebooks. The words were taken from Zion Songster, seventh edition, 1832, by Mason, but are supposed to have been composed about 1779 by William Cowper. The note also identifies a tune by Oliver Bronson under the title “Virginia,” page 191.

145t.title: Warrenton
145t.firstLine: Come, thou fount of ev'ry blessing, Tune my heart to sing thy grace;
145t.scriptureReference: “And shall lead them unto living fountains of waters.”—Rev. 7:17
145t.historicalNote: The heading credits the bass and tenor to J. Williams and the treble to William Walker, 1835. The tune was published in Southern Harmony by William Walker, 1835, page 94, and is described as an old tune. The alto was added by S. M. Denson in 1911.

145b.title: Sweet Affliction
145b.firstLine: In the floods of tribulation, While the billows o'er me roll,
145b.scriptureReference: “In the world ye shall have tribulation, but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world.”—John 16:33

146.title: Hallelujah
146.firstLine: And let this feeble body fail, And let it faint or die;
146.scriptureReference: “Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his.”—Num. 23:10
146.historicalNote: The hymn was published in the second series of Charles Wesley's Funeral Hymns and originally had nine stanzas. The note gives brief biographical information on Wesley.

147t.title: Boylston
147t.firstLine: My God, my life, my love, To thee, to thee I call;
147t.scriptureReference: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee.”—Psa. 73:25
147t.historicalNote: The original title of the hymn was “God All in All,” in Spiritual Songs, book two, published 1707 by Dr. Watts. The note says the tune is claimed by some to have been originally composed by Lowell Mason and that, in its present form, it was either composed or rearranged by him among other tunes he produced in 1832.

147b.title: Laban
147b.firstLine: My soul, be on thy guard; Ten thousand foes arise;
147b.scriptureReference: “For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not wickedly departed from my God.”—II Sam. 22:22
147b.historicalNote: The note gives biographical information on George Heath and describes Laban as one of Lowell Mason's standard hymn tunes.

148.title: Jefferson
148.firstLine: Glorious things of thee are spoken, Zion, city of our God!
148.scriptureReference: “New Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God.”—Rev. 3:12
148.historicalNote: Jefferson appeared in Southern Harmony, 1835, page 42; Missouri Harmony, 1827 and 1837, page 55; and many earlier song books. The note states that the printing is otherwise essentially unchanged except for the alto composed by S. M. Denson in 1911. The words are by John Newton and appear in Olney's Hymns, page 206.

149.title: The Trumpet
149.firstLine: The chariot! the chariot! its wheels roll in fire,
149.scriptureReference: “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”—1 Cor. 15:52
149.historicalNote: The historical note calls the tune “Triumph,” although the page heading reads “The Trumpet.” It says “Triumph” is credited to J. Williams in Southern Harmony, 1835, page 57; the 1849 edition on the same page; and Christian Harmony, page 357.

150.title: The Spiritual Sailor
150.firstLine: The people called Christians, Have many things to tell About the land of Canaan, Where saints and angels dwell;
150.scriptureReference: “Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God on this behalf.”—Peter 4:16

151.title: Symphony
151.firstLine: Behold the Judge descends, his guards are nigh; Tempests and fire attend him down the sky;
151.scriptureReference: “For the hour of his judgement has come, and worship him that made heaven, and earth, and sea.”—Rev. 14:7
151.historicalNote: Described as one of the oldest American tunes. The note cites Missouri Harmony, page 84, and states that it has appeared in each revision of The Sacred Harp since 1844. It also appears on page 40 of John Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, published in 1810, where it is credited to R. D. Munson. The editors conclude that Munson probably composed it about 1810 and provide biographical information about him.

152.title: Shepherds Rejoice
152.firstLine: Shepherds rejoice! lift up your eyes, And send your fears away,
152.historicalNote: The page states that the tune was rearranged by B. S. Aiken in 1908. The words are described as part of those used with the tune “Oxford” in The Sacred Harp and as originally appearing in the Methodist Hymn Book, page 425.

153.title: Resurrected
153.firstLine: My father's gone to view that land, My father's gone to view that land,
153.scriptureReference: “And they ascended up to heaven in a cloud.”—Rev. 11:12
153.historicalNote: The heading credits S. M. D., 1908, at left and S. M. Denson, 1908, at right, with treble by Mrs. Sidney Denson. The historical note instead states that Professor Denson arranged the words in 1903 and applied them to music composed at the same date. It instructs singers to substitute mother, brother, and sister for other verses. First published in the Union Harp and History of Songs by J. S. James, 1909.

154.title: Rest for the Weary
154.firstLine: Come, Thy Fount of ev'ry blessing, Tune my heart to sing Thy grace:
154.scriptureReference: “I will sing unto the Lord; I will sing praise to the Lord God of Israel.”—Judge 5:3
154.historicalNote: The heading says “Original Arrangement by B. F. W. 1869.” The note says the tune was rearranged by Major B. F. White in 1869 for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp and that its air is an old melody found in early American song books. The heading credits Robert Robinson, while the biographical note calls him John Robinson.

155.title: Northfield
155.firstLine: How long, dear Saviour, O how long Shall this bright hour delay?
155.scriptureReference: “I say unto you, hereafter ye shall see heaven open.”—John 1:51
155.historicalNote: Biographical note on Jeremiah Ingalls, born in Massachusetts in 1764 and died in 1828. His Christian Harmony was published in 1804 and contained about thirty of his own tunes. Northfield is one of three tunes on the page discussed as settings of related hymn texts.

156.title: Jesus Rose
156.firstLine: Go and tell His disciples, Go and tell His disciples,
156.scriptureReference: “That He is risen from the dead.”—Matt. 28:7
156.historicalNote: The page states “Arranged by H. S. R., 1869” and credits H. S. Reese, 1869.

157.title: Essay
157.firstLine: See how the wicked kingdom Is falling ev'ry day!
157.historicalNote: The tune was composed by A. C. Clark for Southern Harmony in 1835, page 255, and appeared in The Sacred Harp from 1844 to 1869. The words are said to have appeared consistently in the books consulted and to have been taken from Baptist Harmony, page 455. Clark was related to William Walker and B. F. White.

158.title: Funeral Thought
158.firstLine: Thou art gone to the grave, but we will not deplore thee,
158.scriptureReference: “And there shall be no night there, and they need no candle, neither light of the sun, for the Lord God giveth them light.”—Rev. 22:5
158.historicalNote: The page identifies the text as “On the Death of an Infant.” The note says Bishop Reginald Heber composed the hymn on the death of his only child and describes it as a hymn of resignation and faith in the resurrection of the dead.

159.title: Wondrous Love
159.firstLine: What wondrous love is this! oh, my soul! oh, my soul!
159.scriptureReference: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him, should not perish, but have everlasting life.”—John 3:16
159.historicalNote: The page explicitly states that the authorship of both the words and music is unknown.

160t.title: War Department
160t.firstLine: No more shall the sound of the war-whoop be heard,
160t.historicalNote: The tune is believed to have been composed soon after one of the wars with the Indians. The editors suppose it was composed about 1835 but found no author named in the books consulted. It was first published in Southern Harmony by William Walker in 1835, page 94, and also appeared in Social Harp, page 167.

160b.title: Turn, Sinner, Turn.
160b.firstLine: Today, if you will hear his voice, Now is the time to make your choice;
160b.scriptureReference: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath.”—Eph. 4:26
160b.historicalNote: The note identifies Prof. E. J. King as author of the music. The words are found in Loyd's Hymn Book, page 118, published in 1858, and in Mercer's Cluster, page 165, editions of 1823 and 1830.

161.title: Sweet Home
161.firstLine: 'Mid scenes of confusion and creature complaints, How sweet to my soul is communion with saints;
161.scriptureReference: “We rejoice by faith in hope of the glory of God.”—Rom. 5:2
161.historicalNote: The note discusses the history of “Sweet Home,” its association with John Howard Payne's opera Clara, the Maid of Milan, and the attribution of the music to Sir Henry Bishop. It notes that Payne was the author of the words.

162.title: Plenary
162.firstLine: Hark! from the tombs a doleful sound, Mine ears, attend the cry;
162.scriptureReference: “Marvel not at this, for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice.”—John 5:28
162.historicalNote: Plenary is credited to A. Clark in The Sacred Harp beginning in 1844 and in revisions through 1869. The note states that A. Clark and A. C. Clark are believed to be the same person and that the tune has retained page 162 since the original 1844 book.

163.title: Morning
163.firstLine: He dies, the friend of sinners dies,
163.scriptureReference: “But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins.”—Mark 2:10
163.historicalNote: The heading cites the Psalmist, 232nd Hymn. The hymn was first published by Watts in 1709 under the title “Christ Dying, Raising and Reigning”; John Wesley later altered portions of the text. The note gives biographical information on Henry K. Oliver and several of his compositions.

164.title: Duane Street
164.firstLine: A poor way-faring man of grief hath often crossed me on my way;
164.scriptureReference: “For I hungered and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty and ye gave me drink; I was a stranger and ye took me in, naked and ye clothed me.”—Matt. 25:35-36
164.historicalNote: The original title of the hymn was “The Stranger.” The note states that the text has been set to many tunes but is more closely associated with Cole's “Duane Street” than with any other music.

165.title: Family Bible
165.firstLine: How painfully pleasing the fond recollection Of youthful connection and innocent joy,
165.scriptureReference: “And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished.”—Deu. 31:24
165.historicalNote: Described as one of the old minor melodies. Its source could not be definitely traced, although words and portions of the tune occur in song books from early in the nineteenth century.

166.title: Still Better
166.firstLine: Teach me how to do my duty In the service of my Lord,

musicAttribution.credit: Israel Bradfield and J. L. Meggs

166.scriptureReference: “And the chief priests and scribes stood and vehemently accused him.”—Luke 23:10
166.historicalNote: Israel Bradfield and J. L. Meggs are said to have lived in southwestern Alabama. Bradfield is identified as a close relative of Oliver Bradfield.

167.title: Pray, Brethren, Pray.
167.firstLine: Pray, brethren, pray, the prayer of th availeth;
167.scriptureReference: “I will pray with the spirit and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.”—1 Cor. 14:15
167.historicalNote: The tune is taken from Zion Minstrel, one of the early hymn books, but its author is unknown. The music is described as an old melody and was prepared and arranged for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp.

168.title: Cowper
168.firstLine: Forgive the song that falls so low, Beneath the gratitude I owe.
168.scriptureReference: “Singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord,”—Col. 3:16

169.title: Dartmouth
169.firstLine: Come sound his praise abroad, And hymns of glory sing,
169.scriptureReference: “Singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.”—Eph. 5:19
169.historicalNote: The composer is unknown. The note reports two dates associated with Watts's composition of the hymn, 1704 and 1719, and describes the tune as old, appearing in song books early in the nineteenth century.

170.title: Exhilaration
170.firstLine: Oh! may I worthy prove to see The saints in full prosperity,
170.scriptureReference: “And washed us from our sins in his own blood.”—Rev. 1:5
170.historicalNote: Dr. T. W. Carter is credited with several tunes in the volume, although the note says little was known about him after the War between the States.

171.title: Exhortation
171.firstLine: Lord, in the morning thou shalt hear My voice ascending high;
171.scriptureReference: “My precious voice thou shalt hear in the morning, O Lord, in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee.”—Ps. 5:3

172.title: Harmony
172.firstLine: Wake, all ye soaring throngs, and sing, Ye cheerful warblers of the spring,
172.scriptureReference: “Praise ye the Lord; beasts, and all cattle; creeping things, and flying fowl.”—148 Ps. 9:10
172.historicalNote: Hall was born in Massachusetts in 1785. He was a farmer, manufactured straw bonnets, kept a hotel, and taught a singing school. Music was an avocation, but he composed a number of tunes and was described as almost self-taught.

173.title: Phoebus
173.firstLine: Lord, in the morning thou shall hear My voice ascending high;
173.scriptureReference: “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.”—Ps. 55:17

174.title: Petersburg
174.firstLine: Thus saith the high and lofty One I sit upon my holy throne,
174.scriptureReference: “Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion endureth throughout all generations.”—Ps. 145:13
174.historicalNote: Petersburg is described as an old tune appearing in early nineteenth-century song books, none of which consulted by the editors named its author. It had appeared in The Sacred Harp since 1844 without change. The editors also state that they could find no trace of the words in the books consulted.

175.title: Highlands of Heaven
175.firstLine: Sinner, go, will you go, To the highlands of heaven;
175.scriptureReference: “My kingdom is not of this world.”—John 18:36
175.historicalNote: The note states that Arnold composed three tunes in The Sacred Harp—Shady Grove, Highlands of Heaven, and Zion's Ship—but gives no further information about him or the words.

176t.title: Ragan
176t.firstLine: Farewell, vain world, I'm going home; I belong to this band, Hallelujah.
176t.scriptureReference: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”—Ps. 116:15
176t.historicalNote: The heading says “Arr. by W. F. Moore, Oct. 12, 1869.” An author's note states: “I learned the Air of the above piece of music from the Rev. R. G. Ragan, of Davisville, Ala.”

176b.title: Blooming Youth
176b.firstLine: In the bright season of thy youth, In nature's smiling bloom,
176b.scriptureReference: “Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth.”—Ec. 12:1

177.title: The Christian's Flight
177.firstLine: Not many years their rounds shall roll; Each moment brings it nigh,
177.scriptureReference: “I will bless the Lord at all times: His praise shall continually be in my mouth.”—Ps. 34:1
177.historicalNote: The page states “Words Rearranged by W. F. Moore, 1866.” The biographical note identifies Moore as the first president of the Tallapoosa Singing Convention and a member of the Southern Musical Convention. The editors state that the time of his birth and death was unknown.

178.title: Hosana
178.firstLine: When, his salvation bringing, To Zion Jesus came;
178.scriptureReference: “Children crying in the temple, and saying, Hosana to the Son of David.”—Matt. 21:15
178.historicalNote: Americh Hall is identified as the author of the tune. The note says he was born at Raynham, Massachusetts, in 1785 and died there in 1827; he farmed, manufactured straw bonnets, kept a tavern, and taught singing schools.

179.title: The Christian Warfare
179.firstLine: I find myself placed in a state of probation, Which God has commanded us well to improve;
179.scriptureReference: “In the world ye shall have tribulation; but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”—John 16:33
179.historicalNote: Described as an old tune probably composed in the latter eighteenth or early nineteenth century. It appears in Southern Harmony, 1835, page 37, and Christian Harmony, page 363. The editors state that none of the books consulted names the author of the words or music.

180.title: Vermont
180.firstLine: In vain we lavish out our lives, To gather empty wind;
180.scriptureReference: “For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats.”—Heb. 13:9
180.historicalNote: Described as one of the older melodies and probably printed very early in the eighteenth century. The note cites Missouri Harmony, 1837, Allen D. Carden's Supplement of 1827, and The Sacred Harp beginning in 1844.

181.title: Exit
181.firstLine: Death, like an overflowing stream, Sweeps us away; our life's a dream,
181.scriptureReference: “He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down.”—Job 14:2

182.title: Newburgh
182.firstLine: Let every creature join To praise th' eternal God;
182.scriptureReference: “Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord. Praise ye the Lord.”—Ps. 150:6
182.historicalNote: The note traces Newburgh through Southern Harmony, Missouri Harmony, Christian Harmony, Lute of Zion, and other books. The oldest source the editors found was Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, 1810, page 41, where Munson is credited as author.

183.title: Greenwich
183.firstLine: Lord, what a thoughtless wretch was I, To mourn, and murmur, and repine,
183.historicalNote: The editors describe Greenwich as an old tune found in Presbyterian Psalmist, page 364, and in Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, 1810, page 108. They believe it considerably older than those printings. The tune had appeared in The Sacred Harp from 1844 through 1869 and was first published in Daniel Read's Columbian Harmony in 1793.

184.title: Enfield
184.firstLine: Before the rosy dawn of day, To thee, my God I'll sing;
184.scriptureReference: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.”—1 Cor. 14:15
184.historicalNote: The tune is credited to S. Chandler in Presbyterian Psalmist, page 121, a book published early in the nineteenth century. The note says the copyright and other dates are gone.

185.title: Pilgrim's Farewell
185.firstLine: Farewell, farewell, farewell, my friends, I must be gone, I have no home or stay with you,
185.scriptureReference: “Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace.”—2 Cor. 13:11
185.historicalNote: Described as one of the old melodies, published early in the nineteenth century. The editors state that its author is not named in any of the books they consulted.

186.title: Sherburne
186.firstLine: While shepherds watch'd their flocks by night, All seated on the ground,
186.scriptureReference: “And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night.”—Luke 2:8

187.title: Protection
187.firstLine: God, my supporter, and my hope, My help forever near;
187.scriptureReference: “He hath shewed strength with his arm; he hath scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.”—Luke 1:51
187.historicalNote: The heading says the tune was rearranged by Rollin H. Sherman about 1835. The note below says Sherman rearranged it sometime between 1830 and 1844 and refers readers to Exit, page 181, for further remarks. The page prints the opening stanza and also stanzas numbered 5 and 6.

188.title: Spring
188.firstLine: The scatter'd clouds are fled at last, The rain is gone, the winter's past;
188.scriptureReference: “Let the inhabitants of the rock sing, let them shout from the top of the mountains.”—Isa. 42:11
188.historicalNote: Spring had appeared in The Sacred Harp since 1844. The note also cites Lute of Zion by T. B. Woodbury, 1856, and a recopyright by Mrs. M. A. Woodbury in 1881, page 217. It describes Spring as a lively melody requiring close attention to render correctly.

189.title: Montgomery
189.firstLine: Early my God, without delay, I haste to seek thy face;
189.scriptureReference: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them.”—Eccl. 12:1
189.historicalNote: The historical note presents two competing claims for the tune: one associated with “Moore” and the other with Rev. David Morgan, a Presbyterian minister. The visible text ends with the editors stating that they are satisfied Morgan is—, but the conclusion of that sentence is not present in this scan. The heading credits Rev. David Morgan, about 1805.

191.title: Virginia
191.firstLine: Thy words the raging winds control, And rule the boist'rous deep;
191.scriptureReference: “He sendeth out his word, and melteth them: he causeth his wind to blow, and the waters flow.”—147 Ps. 18
191.historicalNote: Oliver Bronson is identified as the author of Virginia. In 1783 he published Select Tunes and Anthems, which contained original pieces including Virginia, Invitation, and Jubilee.

192.title: Schenectady
192.firstLine: From all that dwell below the skies, Let the Creator's praise arise;
192.scriptureReference: “O sing unto the Lord a new song: sing unto the Lord, all the earth.”—Ps. 96:1
192.historicalNote: Nehemiah Shumway of Philadelphia published The American Harmony in 1801, containing 220 pages and a concise Singer's Manuel. Many of its tunes were his own compositions, and Schenectady is described as one of his best.

193.title: Huntington
193.firstLine: Lord, what a thoughtless wretch was I to mourn, and murmur, and repine;
193.scriptureReference: “Wait on the Lord, and keep his way, and he shall exalt thee to inherit the land.”—Ps. 37:34
193.historicalNote: The heading credits Justin Morgan. The historical note, however, describes Huntington as an older melody appearing in Missouri Harmony, Southern Harmony, Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, and The Sacred Harp, and states that none of those books gives the name of the author of the music.

195.title: Worcester
195.firstLine: How beauteous are their feet Who stand on Zion's hill;
195.scriptureReference: “Ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.”—Luke 13:85
195.historicalNote: Described as one of the oldest American tunes, although some claimed it was an English tune older than the generation of Billings and other American composers. It appeared in the first Sacred Harp in 1844 and revisions through 1869, as well as Missouri Harmony and other American publications.

196.title: Alabama
196.firstLine: Angels in shining order stand, Around the Saviour's throne;
196.scriptureReference: “Make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise.”—Psa. 98:4
196.historicalNote: Alabama is described as one of the old American tunes, composed in the early part of the nineteenth century.

197.title: Georgia
197.firstLine: The cross of Christ inspires my heart To sing redeeming grace,
197.historicalNote: The tune was composed by T. B. McGraw for the 1936 Denson Revision. The note refers to page 558 for additional information.
197.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

198.title: Green Street
198.firstLine: All hail the pow'r of Jesus name! Let angels prostrate fall;
198.scriptureReference: “Thou shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord.”—Isa. 62:3
198.historicalNote: The heading credits J. J. Husband, about 1809. The biographical note beneath the tune instead calls him “J. J. Hubard,” stating that he was born in Plymouth, England, came to the United States in 1809, settled in Pennsylvania, taught music in Philadelphia, served as clerk of St. Paul's Church, and died in Philadelphia in 1825.

200.title: Edom
200.firstLine: With songs and honours sounding loud, Address the Lord on high,
200.scriptureReference: “Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth, who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains.”—Ps. 147:8
200.historicalNote: Edom appeared in Southern Harmony, 1835 and 1848, page 177, and in earlier nineteenth-century books. Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, 1810, page 42, is also cited. The tune was composed by John Cole, born in England in 1774, who came to the United States in 1785, settled in Baltimore, and became a musician and music publisher.

201.title: Pilgrim
201.firstLine: Come, all ye mourning pilgrims dear,
201.scriptureReference: “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.”—2 Tim. 2:3

202.title: New Lebanon
202.firstLine: Great God, the heav'n's well-order'd frame Declares the glories of thy name;
202.scriptureReference: “Let the heaven and earth praise him, the seas, and everything that moveth therein.”—Ps. 69:34
202.historicalNote: Some musicians claimed P. Sherman as the author. The editors state that they believe this attribution is mistaken and that the tune was composed by Roland Sherman, who died in Vermont and was a teacher of music of considerable reputation.

203.title: Florida
203.firstLine: Let sinners take their course, And choose the road to death;
203.scriptureReference: “And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved.”—Acts. 2—21

204.title: Mission
204.firstLine: Young people, all attention give, While I address you in God's name;
204.scriptureReference: “Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth.”—Ecc. 11-9

205.title: Pleasant Hill
205.firstLine: Religion is the chief concern Of mortals here below;
205.scriptureReference: “Therefore shall ye keep my commandments, and do them.”—Lev. 22-31
