205.historicalNote: The tune had appeared in The Sacred Harp since 1844. The note cites Southern Harmony by William Walker, 1835, page 167; Social Harp by John G. McCurry, 1855, page 180; and New Harp of Columbia by M. L. Swan, which credits Nicholson with the music.

206.title: Christian's Hope
206.firstLine: We have our troubles here below, We're trav'ling through this world of woe
206.scriptureReference: “Lord Jesus Christ, which is our hope.”—I Tim. 1:1
206.historicalNote: H. A. Parris is identified as composer of both the words and music. The note says that in 1911 he resided at Helicon, Alabama, was a great lover of old Sacred Harp tunes, and was a consistent member of the Missionary Baptist Church.

207.title: Louisiana
207.firstLine: Come, little children, now we may partake a little morsel,
207.scriptureReference: “Whosoever shall receive one of such children in my name, receiveth me.”—Mark 9:37

208.title: Traveling On
208.firstLine: Farewell, my loving friends, farewell, I have no home or stay with you;

musicAttribution.credit: S. M. Denson and J. S. James

208.scriptureReference: “I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies, and of all the truth, which thou hast shewed unto thy servant: for with my staff I passed over this Jordan.”—Gen. 32:10
208.historicalNote: The tune was composed for the Fifth Edition of The Sacred Harp in 1911. The words are the same as those used in Pilgrim's Farewell, page 185. The note also cites Southern Harmony, 1835 and 1848, page 158, and Mercer's Cluster, 1823, page 366; none of those sources names the author of the words.

209.title: Evening Shade
209.firstLine: The day is past and gone, The evening shades appear;
209.scriptureReference: “The night cometh when no man can work.”—John 9-4

210.title: Lena
210.firstLine: See the Lord of glory dying! See him gasping! hear him crying!
210.scriptureReference: “Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost.”—Matt. 27:50
210.historicalNote: The tune is described as one of the old melodies appearing in some of the earliest American tune books. The note cites Southern Harmony, 1835 and 1848, page 149; Christian Harmony, 1866, page 270; Timbrel of Zion, page 210; and John Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, 1814 and 1824.

211.title: Whitestown
211.firstLine: Where nothing dwelt but beasts of prey, Or men as fierce and wild as they,
211.scriptureReference: “The good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one.”—Matt. 13:38
211.historicalNote: Described as an old melody of the early nineteenth century. The note cites Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, 1810, page 39; Southern Harmony, 1835, page 135; and Missouri Harmony, 1827 and 1837, page 19. The editors state that they have no data identifying the author of the words. They reject a Sacred Harp attribution to Wm. Ward as a mistake because the tune is considerably older, and note that Wyeth credits the tune to Howell.

212.title: Sharon
212.firstLine: How pleasant 'tis to see Kindred and friends agree,
212.scriptureReference: “And he said, Let me go, I pray thee; for our family hath a sacrifice in the city; and my brother, he hath commanded me to be there.”—1 Sam. 20:29

213t.title: The Good Old Way
213t.firstLine: Lift up your heads, Immanuel's friends, O halle, hallelujah.
213t.scriptureReference: “Let them give glory unto the Lord, and declare his praise.”—Isa. 42:12

213b.title: Warning
213b.firstLine: To-day the Saviour calls, Ye wand'rers, Come!
213b.scriptureReference: “Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling.”—2 Tim. 1:9
213b.historicalNote: The heading additionally describes the tune as “Peculiar.”

214.title: Repentance
214.firstLine: Oh, if my soul was formed for woe, How would I vent my sighs!
214.scriptureReference: “But, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.”—Luke 13:8

215.title: New Topia
215.firstLine: Young people all, attention give, And hear what I do say;
215.scriptureReference: “He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity, and the rod of his anger shall fall.”—Prov. 22:8
215.historicalNote: Described as a great old minor piece, probably printed in early nineteenth-century books. The note cites Missouri Harmony, 1827 and 1837, page 74; Southern Harmony, 1835, page 169; Social Harp, 1855, page 176; and New Harp of Columbia, page 163. All of those books except The Sacred Harp are said to credit the tune to Munday.

216.title: Delight
216.firstLine: No burning heats by day, Nor blasts of evening air, shall take my health away, If God be with me there.
216.scriptureReference: “I will guide thee with mine eye.”—Ps. 32:8
216.historicalNote: The editors state that they were unable to find information about Mr. Coan, the author of the tune. It is described as longstanding and is cited in Southern Harmony, 1835 and 1848, page 167; Missouri Harmony, 1827 and 1837, page 85; and Social Harp, 1855, page 180.

217.title: Ballstown
217.firstLine: Great God, attend, while Zion sings the joy that from thy presence springs;
217.scriptureReference: “O Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer.”—Ps. 84:8
217.historicalNote: Described as one of the old melodies. The hymn originally appeared in Psalmist No. 20, was composed in 1719, and bore the title “God and His Church of Grace and Glory.”

218.title: Mount Pleasant
218.firstLine: There is a house not made with hands, Eternal, and on high,
218.scriptureReference: “We have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heaven.”—2 Cor. 5:1
218.historicalNote: The note identifies James Leach as an English musician born near Lancashire in 1762. In 1789 he published a new set of hymns and psalm tunes and a revised edition in 1794. The note also lists several other collections containing his pieces.

220.title: Mount Zion
220.firstLine: The hill of Zion yields, A thousand sacred sweets,
220.scriptureReference: “I will lift mine eyes to the hills, from whence cometh my help.”—Ps. 121:1
220.historicalNote: The words are identified as the final two verses of the hymn “The men of grace have found.” The editors state that the hymn in this volume is connected with the tune Concord. Although the books consulted credit this tune to Brown, the editors could not determine which Bartholomew Brown composed it.

222.title: Ocean
222.firstLine: Thy works of glory, mighty Lord, That rul'st the boist'rous sea;
222.historicalNote: The tune Ocean was composed by Timothy Swan in 1793 and published that year in his New England Harmony. The note says Swan was born in 1760 at Sheffield, Connecticut, and that the tune appeared in several other books.

223.title: Portuguese Hymn
223.firstLine: Hither, ye faithful, haste with songs of triumph, To Bethlehem haste, the Lord of life to meet;
223.scriptureReference: “Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.”—Matt. 2:2
223.historicalNote: The heading states that the piece is from John F. Wade's Cantus Diversi, 1751.

224.title: Save, Lord, or We Perish.
224.firstLine: When thro' the torn sail the wild tempest is streaming, When o'er the dark wave the red lightning is gleaming,
224.scriptureReference: “Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.”—Luke 7:50
224.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” The note identifies Reginald Heber as the author of the hymn, born in England in 1783 and died in 1826, and refers to Funeral Thought, page 158, for further information.

225.title: Christmas Anthem
225.firstLine: Oh how charming, Oh how charming Are the radiant bands of music,
225.scriptureReference: “And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.”—Luke 1:42
225.historicalNote: Prof. James Denson composed the anthem in 1844. The note says he was probably born about 1820 in Walton County, Georgia, and died out west soon after the Civil War. It also describes the musical Denson family and identifies Rev. L. P. Denson as his brother.

227.title: Ode of Life's Journey
227.firstLine: I began life's journey when young, And the glittering prospect charm'd my eyes;
227.scriptureReference: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men.”—Kings 12:8
227.historicalNote: The ode is said to have been composed by E. J. King in or about 1844 for B. F. White and E. J. King's Sacred Harp. The note mentions conflicting reports about the date of King's death and identifies him as one of the compilers of the 1844 Sacred Harp.

228.title: Masonic Ode
228.firstLine: Sacred to heav'n behold the dome appears: Lo! What august solemnity it wears;
228.scriptureReference: “And she gave the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold.”—2 Chro. 9:9
228.historicalNote: Described as an old ode appearing in some of the earliest American books. The note cites John Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, 1810, page 84, where the author is stated to be unknown. The treble was composed by E. J. King in 1844. The same words also appeared in The Sacred Harp and John G. McCurry's Social Harp, page 222, 1855.

232.title: Baptismal Anthem
232.firstLine: In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea,
232.scriptureReference: “In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea.”—Matt. 3:1-4
232.historicalNote: The note gives biographical information on B. F. White: born in Spartanburg, S.C., in 1800 and died in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1879; moved to Hamilton, Harris County, Georgia, in 1842; and died following injuries from an accident in Atlanta.

234.title: Reverential Anthem
234.firstLine: Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name, Come into his courts, Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness.
234.historicalNote: The anthem was composed by Prof. E. J. King in 1844. The note describes King as a music teacher, singer, member of the Missionary Baptist Church, and participant in the Southern Musical Convention and Chattahoochee Musical Convention. It refers to page 278 for additional information.

235.title: Long Sought Home
235.firstLine: Jerusalem! my happy home! Oh how I long for thee!
235.scriptureReference: “In my father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you.”—St. John 14:2

236.title: Easter Anthem
236.firstLine: The Lord is ris'n indeed! Hallelujah! The Lord is ris'n indeed! Hallelujah!
236.historicalNote: Originally called “An Anthem for Easter.” The note states that the words were taken from the New Testament and Young's Night Thoughts and applied to music composed by William Billings. It gives biographical information on Billings and describes Easter Anthem as one of his standard works; the version printed here is said to be substantially as it appears in Missouri Harmony, published 1835.

240.title: Christian Song
240.firstLine: Mine eyes are now closing to rest, My body must soon be remov'd, And mould'ring, lie buried in dust, No more to be envied or lov'd.
240.scriptureReference: “Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord.”—Rev. 14:13
240.historicalNote: The tune is described as being “on the anthem order.” The note cites Southern Harmony by William Walker, 1835, page 129; Missouri Harmony by Carden, 1827-1837, pages 124-5; Christian Harmony, 1866, pages 380-381; and The Sacred Harp from 1844 through 1869.

242.title: Ode on Science
242.firstLine: The morning sun shines from the east, And spreads his glories to the west,
242.scriptureReference: “The sun arises, and the sun goeth down. And hasteth to his place where he arose.”—Eccl. 1:5
242.historicalNote: Described as one of the oldest pieces in the American song-and-tune-book tradition. The earliest copy before the editors was John Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, where it appears on page 130. The note also cites Missouri Harmony, 1837; Southern Harmony, 1835, page 210; and The Sacred Harp from 1844 through 1869.

245.title: Claremont
245.firstLine: Vital spark of heav'nly flame Quit, oh? quit this mortal frame;
245.scriptureReference: “Oh death, where is thy sting? Oh grave where is thy victory?”—1st Cor. 15:55
245.historicalNote: The hymn is credited to Alexander Pope. The note describes this favorite ode or anthem as a free version of the Emperor Adrian's Address to His Soul When Dying.

250.title: Heavenly Vision
250.firstLine: I beheld, and lo a great multitude, which no man could number:
250.historicalNote: Described as one of the old American anthems appearing in early publications of William Billings. The note identifies Billings as the first American to compose, compile, and publish a sacred song book and states that he was born in Boston in 1746 and died there in 1800.

254.title: Rose of Sharon
254.firstLine: I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valley:
254.historicalNote: The anthem was composed by William Billings. The note describes Billings as an early American composer of sacred music, refers to further biographical information under Funeral Anthem on page 520, and states that this anthem and others were composed in the latter part of the eighteenth century and published in his books from about 1770 to 1800.

260.title: Farewell Anthem
260.firstLine: My friends, I am going a long and tedious journey, Never to return,
260.historicalNote: The note states that this anthem was the last tune in the first edition of The Sacred Harp by White & King, published in 1844, and that it retained the same pages in subsequent revisions.

263.title: Doddridge
263.firstLine: Why, O sinner, me profaning—Why, says God, my statutes name;
263.scriptureReference: “And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear.”—1 Peter 4:18
263.historicalNote: M. Mark Wynn, author of the tune, was a Georgian and taught music for a period from 1865 to 1868.

266.title: Ode on Pious Life
266.firstLine: So let our lives and lips express The holy gospel we profess;
266.scriptureReference: “Ye are the light of the World.”—Matt. 5:14
266.historicalNote: The melody was rearranged by Prof. B. F. White for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp in 1869. The note supposes that White obtained the outlines of the ode from American Harmony, compiled by Oliver Holden and first published in 1793.

268.title: David's Lamentation
268.firstLine: David the king was grieved and moved, He went to his chamber, his chamber, and wept;
268.scriptureReference: “And as he went, thus he said, O my son Absalom! my son, my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son.”—2 Sam. 16:33
268.historicalNote: The tune appeared in early song books by William Billings and is described as one of his early fugue tunes. The note says some claimed that he composed it in 1800; the precise date is uncertain, but the editors place it somewhere near that date.

269.title: Bear Creek
269.firstLine: Lord when Thou didst ascend on high, Ten thousand angels filled the sky,

harmonizationAttribution.credit: B. F. White; G. B. Daniel

269.scriptureReference: “The chariots of God are twenty thousand, even thousands of angels.”—Ps. 67:17
269.historicalNote: The heading states “Arranged by B. F. White. Alto by G. B. Daniel.” The note says the words were fixed in 1911 so they could be sung, and that Major White rearranged the tune in 1869, replacing “All Saints Now.” The original hymn has four verses. Tullis's M. E. Hymn Book, South, 1888, No. 120, is cited.

270.title: Confidence
270.firstLine: Away, my unbelieving fear; Fear shall in me no more have place;
270.scriptureReference: “Repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.”—Acts 20:21
270.historicalNote: Professor James R. Turner is identified as author of both the words and music. The note states that he was born in Hancock County in 1807, died in 1874, taught music in Georgia and Alabama for more than forty years, and helped revise The Sacred Harp in 1858.

271t.title: Arkansas
271t.firstLine: Farewell, farewell to all below; My Saviour calls and I must go;
271t.scriptureReference: “Be ye not conformed to this world.”—Rom. 12:2
271t.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original” and says “For the Organ, by S. P. Barnett, 1869.” The note identifies S. P. Barnett as author of the tune, states that he lived for a long time in Carroll County, Georgia, and died there sometime between 1890 and 1895.

271b.title: Restoration
271b.firstLine: How many years has man been driv'n, Far off from happiness and heav'n;
271b.scriptureReference: “For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church; and he is the Saviour of the body.”—Eph. 5:23
271b.historicalNote: Americh Hall of Massachusetts composed the tune in 1811. The note cites Southern Harmony, 1835 and 1848, page 5, and states that S. M. Denson composed the alto in 1911, one hundred years after the tune was composed.

272.title: Exhortation
272.firstLine: Now, in the heat of youthful blood, Remember your Creator, God!
272.historicalNote: The words were taken from Mercer's Cluster by Jesse Mercer of Powellton, Georgia, Third Edition, published in 1823, page 174. The tune was credited in The Sacred Harp from 1844 through 1869 to Doolittle.

273.title: Milford
273.firstLine: If angels sung a Saviour's birth, If angels sung a Saviour's birth, On that auspicious morn,
273.scriptureReference: “The voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears.”—Luke 1:44
273.historicalNote: The heading gives “J. S. about 1802” at left and “John Stephenson, about 1802” at right. The note states that Sir John Stephenson, author of the music and probably of the words, was born in Ireland in 1772.

274t.title: The Golden Harp
274t.firstLine: Farewell vain world, I'm going home To play on the Golden Harp.
274t.scriptureReference: “Yea, upon the harp will I praise thee.”—Ps. 43:4
274t.historicalNote: The page gives a brief biographical note on Prof. J. P. Reese: born in Jasper County, Georgia, in 1828, died in Coweta County in 1900, and buried at Oak Hill Cemetery, Newnan, Georgia.

274b.title: Roll Jordan
274b.firstLine: He comes! He comes! the Judge severe, Roll, Jordan, roll;

musicAttribution.credit: A. W. and John G. McCurry

274b.scriptureReference: “Blow the trumpet among the nations, prepare the nations.”—Jer. 51:27

275t.title: Loving-Kindness
275t.firstLine: Awake my soul, to joyful lays; Halle, Hallelujah!
275t.scriptureReference: “Praise ye the Lord. Sing unto the Lord a new song, and his praise is in the congregation of saints.”—Ps. 149:1
275t.historicalNote: The tune was composed by J. P. and S. R. Penick for the first Appendix to The Sacred Harp in 1850. The note says they were believed to be brothers. S. M. Denson composed the alto in 1911. A biographical note on Samuel Medley states that he was born in England in 1738, died in 1799, and composed about 230 hymns.

275b.title: Roll On
275b.firstLine: Why should we start and fear to die, What tim'rous worms we mortals are!
275b.scriptureReference: “For the word of the Lord is right; and all his works are done in truth.”—Ps. 33:4

276.title: Bridgewater
276.firstLine: From all that dwell below the skies, Let the Redeemer's praise arise:
276.scriptureReference: “All the earth shall worship thee, and shall sing unto thee; they shall sing to thy name. Selah.”—Ps. 66:4
276.historicalNote: Bridgewater was composed by Lewis Edson in 1782. The note states that Edson was born in 1746 and died in 1820, and cites Presbyterian Psalmist, Missouri Harmony, Lute of Zion, and other older books.

277.title: Antioch
277.firstLine: I know that my Redeemer lives, Glory, Hallelujah!
277.scriptureReference: “For I know that my Redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth.”—Job 19:25
277.historicalNote: The words were first published in Medley's Hymns in 1800 and originally contained nine stanzas. The hymn was composed about 1784. The note identifies U. C. Wood as composer of the music and says little definite was known about him, though B. F. Wilson recalled him as a good man, fine singer, and music director who was killed by a falling tree or limb.

278t.title: Sweet Heaven
278t.firstLine: The Lord who built the earth and sky, In mercy stoops to hear thy cry;
278t.scriptureReference: “Ask and it shall be given you.”—Math. 7:7
278t.historicalNote: The heading credits E. L. King, 1850. The note, however, refers to “E. J. King, junior author of the Sacred Harp,” as the person who set the tune to music and says he died shortly after the 1844 publication. The conflicting initials and chronology are retained rather than reconciled.

278b.title: Traveling Pilgrim
278b.firstLine: Farewell! vain world, I'm going home, Where there's no more stormy clouds to rise.
278b.scriptureReference: “Man goeth to his long sought home.”—Ec. 12:5
278b.historicalNote: The note identifies Rev. H. S. Reese as born in Jasper County, Georgia, in 1827 and then living at Turin, Georgia. He is described as a Missionary Baptist minister who had preached for more than fifty-five years and as a twin brother of Professor J. P. Reese.

279.title: The Shepherd's Flock
279.firstLine: Ye, little flock whom Jesus feeds, Dismiss your anxious fears;
279.historicalNote: Elder Elmer Kitchens of Birmingham, Alabama, composed the music in 1935. The note states that it was his first musical composition and refers to other music by him on pages 512 and 568.
279.copyrightNotice: Copyright, 1936, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc.

280.title: Westford
280.firstLine: Far from my thoughts, vain world, be gone, Let my religious hours alone,
280.scriptureReference: “Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable.”—Heb. 11:12
280.historicalNote: The note refers to the history of Daniel Read under Windham, page 38, and adds that in 1806 he published the Litchfield Collection of Church Music.

282.title: I'm Going Home
282.firstLine: Farewell vain world! I'm going home! My Saviour smiles and bids me come,
282.scriptureReference: “And I will rejoice in Jerusalem, and joy in my people: and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying.”—Isa. 65:19
282.historicalNote: Breedlove is described as a music teacher in Georgia who died in South Georgia about forty years before the note was written. He belonged to the Southern Musical Convention from its organization in 1844 until his death and served as secretary from 1845 to 1850. In the Sacred Harp compiled by B. F. White and E. J. King he is credited with Arnold and ten other tunes.

283.title: Sabbath Morning
283.firstLine: Come, let us join with one accord, In hymns around the throne;
283.historicalNote: The tune was the first musical composition written by H. N. McGraw and was considered by many singers to be his best. It first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 492.
283.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

284.title: Entrekin
284.firstLine: My span of life will soon be gone, The passing moments say;
284.historicalNote: The tune was written in 1935 by L. A. (Lee) McGraw, older brother of H. N. and T. B. McGraw. He is described as an excellent singer and leader.
284.copyrightNotice: Copyright, 1936, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc.

285t.title: Arnold
285t.firstLine: Come let us join our friends above, That have obtain'd the prize
285t.scriptureReference: “And have hope toward God, which they themselves also allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.”—Acts 24:15

285b.title: Land of Rest
285b.firstLine: O land of rest, for thee I sigh, When will the moments come?
285b.scriptureReference: Lord thy God hath given thee rest in the land which the Lord thy God giveth.—Deu. 25-19
285b.historicalNote: The note refers to the history of H. S. Reese under Traveling Pilgrim, page 278, and to other tunes by him in the volume.

286.title: Heavenly Home
286.firstLine: While trav'ling thru the world below, Where sore afflictions come,
286.historicalNote: The heading additionally says “Arr. by W. A. Y.” The note states that the song was written by W. A. Yates for the 1936 Denson Revision. Yates resided in northwest Alabama and was described as one of the most ardent supporters of Sacred Harp music in that section.
286.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

287.title: Cambridge
287.firstLine: The Lord will happiness divine On contrite hearts bestow;
287.scriptureReference: “Draw nigh to God and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye doubleminded.”—James 4:8
287.historicalNote: The editors state that they were unable to find information about Dr. John Randall, author of the music, although Cambridge was a standard tune. It appeared on page 14 of the National Hymn Book of the American Churches by Robert Ellis Thompson, S.T.D.

288.title: White
288.firstLine: Ye fleeting charms of earth farewell, Your springs of joy are dry;
288.scriptureReference: “For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world; and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.”—1 John 5:4
288.historicalNote: The tune was composed in honor of B. F. White. The note refers to other remarks concerning Dumas elsewhere in the volume and says the revisers placed White on this page in 1859, removing Shepherds Rejoice.
288.copyrightNotice: In honor of B. F. White.

289.title: Greensborough
289.firstLine: There is a land of pure delight, where saints immortal reign;
289.historicalNote: The note states that the hymn appears as No. 87 in Rev. Lewis Benson's compilation of church hymns and describes it as one of the best and most widely approved hymns among Christian denominations.

290.title: Victoria
290.firstLine: Alas! and did my Saviour bleed? Alas! and did my Saviour bleed? And did my Saviour die?
290.scriptureReference: “Christ Jesus came to save sinners.”—1 Tim. 1:15
290.historicalNote: Victoria was credited to Leonard P. Breedlove for the 1859 revision of the second appendix to The Sacred Harp. The note says Breedlove probably rearranged rather than originally composed the tune, because it appears in Carden's Missouri Harmony, 1837, page 206.

291.title: Majesty
291.firstLine: The Lord descended from above, And bow'd the heav'ns most high;
291.scriptureReference: “And behold, there was a great earthquake: for the angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone from the door, and sat upon it.”—Matt. 28-2
291.historicalNote: The note gives biographical information on William Billings, identifying him as a Boston-born, self-taught musician and composer whose works include New England Psalm Singer, Billings' Best, Heavenly Vision, Rose of Sharon, and many other anthems.

292.title: Behold the Savior
292.firstLine: Behold the Savior of mankind Nailed to the shameful tree!
292.historicalNote: Paine Denson, older son of Thomas J. Denson, composed the tune. It first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 524.
292.copyrightNotice: Copyrighted, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

293.title: Akers
293.firstLine: When I can read my title clear To mansions in the skies,
293.historicalNote: The tune first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision. It was composed by Thomas J. Denson, who gave it his last wife's maiden name. See pages 426 and 427. In addition to the two numbered Watts stanzas, the page prints the additional texts beginning “Should earth against my soul engage” and “When we've been there ten thousand years.”
293.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

294.title: Rocky Road
294.firstLine: I'm enlisted on the road, I'm almost done traveling,
294.historicalNote: The heading credits J. C. Brown with the tune and states “Arr. by Paine Denson, 1935.” The page instructs: “For other verses use Mother, Brother, Sister, Etc.”

295.title: Odem
295.firstLine: Let ev'ry mortal ear attend, And ev'ry heart rejoice;
295.historicalNote: Leon McGraw, youngest son of L. A. McGraw, composed the tune. It first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision. The note states that Leon McGraw was on the faculty of Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama.
295.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

296.title: Sardinia
296.firstLine: Behold the love—the gen'rous love That holy David shows!
296.scriptureReference: “Then said Jesus, Father forgive them; for they know not what they do.”—Luke 23-34
296.historicalNote: G. Castil is identified as author of the tune. The note says he was born at Montefiascon in 1721 and died in Paris in 1808. The exact date of Sardinia was unknown but was sometime during the eighteenth century; it is described as one of the oldest melodies and as appearing in early American song books.

297.title: Conversion
297.firstLine: When God reveal'd his gracious name, And changed my mournful state,
297.scriptureReference: “And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.”—John 1-16
297.historicalNote: After diligent search the editors were unable to identify the author of the tune. It is described as an old, longstanding melody, published in The Sacred Harp by B. F. White in 1850 and in earlier song books, none of which consulted named its author.

298.title: Providence
298.firstLine: What shall I render to my God For all his kindness shown?
298.scriptureReference: “To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.”—Luke 1—79

299.title: New Jerusalem
299.firstLine: Lo, what a glorious sight appears To our believing eyes;
299.scriptureReference: “And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven.”—Rev. 21:2

300.title: Calvary
300.firstLine: My thoughts, that often mount the skies, Go, search the world beneath,
300.scriptureReference: “But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God.”—1 Cor. 2-14
300.historicalNote: The tune was composed by Daniel Reed in 1806 and published that year in his Litchfield's Collection of church music, which contained about 112 pages.

301.title: Greenland
301.firstLine: With songs and honors sounding loud, Address the Lord on high,
301.scriptureReference: Who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains.—Ps. 147:8
301.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” The note refers to the account of W. F. Moore under The Christian's Flight, page 177, and explicitly states that Moore is author of the music except for the alto by S. M. Denson in 1911.

302.title: Logan
302.firstLine: The day is past and gone, The evening shades appear;
302.historicalNote: The note identifies John Leland as a Baptist minister, born in 1754 and died in 1844, and refers to biographical sketches on pages 85 and 319 and to T. J. Denson on page 427.

303.title: Love
303.firstLine: O for a closer walk with God, A calm and heav'nly frame,

304.title: Morgan
304.firstLine: With songs and honours sounding loud, Address the Lord on high!
304.scriptureReference: “My doctrine shall be as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass.”—Deut. 32:2
304.historicalNote: After diligent search, the editors were unable to identify the author of the tune. It had been in The Sacred Harp since the revision of 1850.

306.title: Oxford
306.firstLine: Shepherds, rejoice! lift up your eyes, And send your fears away:
306.scriptureReference: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given.”—Isa. 9:6
306.historicalNote: The note refers to fuller information on John Massengale elsewhere in the volume and states that the hymn used here is the same as that in Shepherds Rejoice, page 479 in the appendix.

308.title: Parting Friends
308.firstLine: What is there here to court my stay, And keep me back from home,
308.scriptureReference: “And to wait for his son from heaven.”—1 Thess. 1:10
308.historicalNote: E. L. King is described as having served on the committee preparing the first appendix to The Sacred Harp in 1850 and on the revision committee. He was a close relative of E. J. King and contributed three tunes to the appendix, including Parting Friends.

309.title: Living Lamb
309.firstLine: Am I a soldier of the cross, A foll'wer of the Lamb?
309.scriptureReference: “Endure hardships as a soldier of Jesus Christ.”—2 Tim. 2:3

310.title: Weeping Saviour
310.firstLine: Alas and did my saviour bleed! And did my sov'reign die!
310.scriptureReference: “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.”—Eph. 1—7
310.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Qriginal.” The note states that Elder E. Dumas composed it in 1839 for the first edition of The Sacred Harp. The original title of the hymn is given as “Godly Sorrow arising from the suffering of Christ.”

311.title: Silver Street
311.firstLine: Come sound his praise abroad, and hymns of glory sing,
311.scriptureReference: “O come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the Lord our maker.”—Ps. 95:6
311.historicalNote: The original title of the hymn is given as “Psalms before Service.” It has six stanzas and is based on the ninety-fifth Psalm. Silver Street was composed by Isaac Smith, an English composer born in London about 1735 and died there about 1800.

312t.title: Sing to Me of Heaven
312t.firstLine: Oh, sing to me of heav'n When I am called to die,
312t.scriptureReference: “I will sing with the Spirit.”—1 Cor. 14:15
312t.historicalNote: Mrs. Mary Stanley Bunce Dana was born in Beaufort, S.C., in 1810 and died in Texas in 1883. The hymn was written in 1840 on the death of a pious friend. The note states that Prof. John Massengale wrote the melody sometime between 1860 and 1869 and that S. M. Denson added the alto in 1911.

312b.title: Restoration
312b.firstLine: Come, thou fount of ev'ry blessing, Tune my heart to sing thy grace;

harmonizationAttribution.credit: T. B. Newton & S. W. Everett

312b.scriptureReference: “We shall receive the blessings from the Lord.”—Ps. 24:5
312b.historicalNote: The heading states “Re-arr. by T. B. Newton & S. W. Everett, 1908” and “Da Capo for Chorus.” The note says Robinson was born in England in 1735, was ordained a Methodist minister, and died in 1797.

313.title: Concord
313.firstLine: The men of grace have found Glory begun below;
313.scriptureReference: “Which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.”—Col. 1:27
313.historicalNote: Oliver Holden is described as a self-taught Massachusetts musician and carpenter who composed hymns and tunes and published several books, including American Harmony and Union Harmony. He later participated with Hans Gram and Samuel Holyoke in publishing the Massachusetts Compiler.

314.title: Cleburne
314.firstLine: All hail the power of Jesus' name, Let angels prostrate fall;
314.scriptureReference: “A royal diadem in the hands of God.”—Isa. 62:3
314.historicalNote: The hymn was written by Rev. Edward Perronett about 1779 and was first published about that time. The note connects it with Coronation and gives an extended biographical account of Prof. S. M. Denson.

315.title: Worlds Above
315.firstLine: Lord of the world above, How pleasant and how fair
315.scriptureReference: “And be not conformed to this world.”—Rom. 12:2
315.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

316.title: New Hope
316.firstLine: Jesus, what shall I do to show How much I love Thy charming name?
316.scriptureReference: “Greater love than this hath no man.”—John 15:13
316.historicalNote: The heading explicitly says “Words arranged by A. M. C. 1908.” The note identifies A. M. Cagle as then living in Winston County, Alabama, and as a pupil of S. M. and T. J. Denson and son-in-law of T. J. Denson.

317.title: Jackson
317.firstLine: I am a stranger here below, And what I am is hard to know,
317.scriptureReference: “They were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.”—Heb. 11:13

318.title: Present Joys
318.firstLine: We thank the Lord of heav'n and earth, Who hath preserved us from our birth,
318.historicalNote: The heading says “Rearranged by A. M. C., 1908.” The note states that the tune was first published in Union Harp and History of Songs by J. S. James in 1909 and had proven a favorite with many singers.

319.title: Religion Is a Fortune
319.firstLine: O when shall I see Jesus, And reign with him above?
319.scriptureReference: “The righteous shall go into life eternal.”—Matt. 25:46
319.historicalNote: The printed music credit is William L. Williams, followed by an indistinct date beginning with “17”; I have not supplied the unreadable digits. The note gives biographical information on John Leland, born in 1754 and died in 1844, describing him as a Baptist minister and hymn writer.

320.title: Funeral Anthem
320.firstLine: I heard a great voice from heav'n saying unto me,
320.historicalNote: The words are taken from Revelation 14:13. The note states that William Billings was born in Boston in 1746 and died there in 1800.

321.title: Newman
321.firstLine: Vain man, thy fond pursuits forbear, Repent, thy end is nigh;
321.scriptureReference: “But except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.”—Luke 13:3
321.historicalNote: The heading states “Music original, by J. P. Rees.”

322.title: Man's Redemption
322.firstLine: The glorious plan of man's redemption, By the Son of God was wrought,
322.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original” and also says “Arranged by S. M. B.” S. M. Brown composed three other tunes in the volume and is described as a singing leader and music director associated with Primitive Baptist churches.

323t.title: Mullins
323t.firstLine: Jesus grant us all a blessing; Send it down, Lord, from above:
323t.scriptureReference: “The blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich.”—Prov. 10:22
323t.historicalNote: Composed by Edward E. Dumas in honor of Elder John Mullins, a Primitive Baptist preacher and friend of Dumas. The words were taken from Zion Songster, page 268, hymn No. 228, in the 1832 seventh edition by Rev. Thomas Mason. The note states that the tune Griffin was removed and Mullins inserted in its place in 1869.

323b.title: Soft Music
323b.firstLine: Soft, soft music is stealing—Sweet, sweet, lingers the strain;

harmonizationAttribution.credit: B. F. White; S. M. Denson

323b.scriptureReference: “Sing songs of Moses and of the Lamb.”—Rev. 15:3
323b.historicalNote: The heading says “Arr. by B. F. White, 1850. Alto by S. M. Denson, 1911.” The note gives biographical information on Mrs. Mary Stanley Bunce Dana, born in Beaufort, S.C., in 1810 and died in Texas in 1883.

324.title: North Port
324.firstLine: Jesus, my all to heav'n has gone, Glory Hallelujah;
324.scriptureReference: “The Lord sat on the right hand of God.”—Mark 16-19
324.historicalNote: The heading specifically credits “Bass by J. Smith, 1859.”

325.title: Soldier of the Cross
325.firstLine: Am I a soldier of the cross, A follower of the Lamb,
325.scriptureReference: “Endure hardships as a soldier of Jesus Christ.”—2 Tim. 2:3
325.historicalNote: The note states that the words were composed by Isaac Watts.

326.title: Weary Pilgrim
326.firstLine: Come and taste, along with me, The weary pilgrim's consolation;
326.scriptureReference: “And ye shall find rest unto your souls.”—Matt. 11:29
326.historicalNote: Leonard P. Breedlove is identified as author of the tune and as having nine other tunes in the book. The note reports traditions that he died in South Georgia about thirty years earlier and states that he assisted in the 1850 revision of The Sacred Harp.

327.title: Invitation
327.firstLine: Hark! the Redeemer from on high, Sweetly invites his fav'rites nigh,
327.scriptureReference: “He is able also to save to the uttermost that come unto God by him.”—Heb. 7:25
327.historicalNote: The tune is taken from M. L. Swan's New Harp of Columbia, page 178, where it is credited to Kimball. The note traces it to Jacob Kimball's Royal Harmony, 1793, and states that it was rearranged by Denson and James in 1911.

328.title: Praise God
328.firstLine: Oh, for a heart to praise my God, A heart from sin set free;
328.scriptureReference: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”—Matt. 5:8
328.historicalNote: The tune was composed by S. M. Denson on April 27, 1911, for the fifth edition of The Original Sacred Harp. The words were selected and arranged in this tune by J. S. James. The note states that the tune is entirely original.

329.title: Vain World Adieu
329.firstLine: When for eternal worlds we steer, And seas are calm and skies are clear,
329.scriptureReference: “Hear this, all ye people, give ear, all ye inhabitants of the world.”—Ps. 49d
329.historicalNote: Elder E. Dumas composed the tune in 1856. The scripture citation is printed as “Ps. 49d” and is retained as printed.

330t.title: Horton
330t.firstLine: My span of life will soon be gone, The passing moments say;
330t.historicalNote: The heading says “Arr. by P. D.” The note states that Paine Denson wrote the tune for the 1936 Denson Revision, that he always arranged the words, and that he gave the tune his second wife's maiden name. See page 524.
330t.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

330b.title: Fellowship
330b.firstLine: Blest be the tie that binds, Our hearts in Christian love;
330b.historicalNote: The tune was composed by Paine Denson and first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision. See footnote on page 524.
330b.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

331.title: Jester
331.firstLine: If our fathers want to go, Why don't they come along? I belong to this band, Hallelujah.
331.scriptureReference: “How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation.”—Heb. 2:3
331.historicalNote: The note states that the words were composed by Prof. Denson in their present shape.

332.title: Sons of Sorrow
332.firstLine: Hail ye sighing sons of sorrow, Learn with me, your certain doom;
332.scriptureReference: “The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away.”—Isa. 24:4
332.historicalNote: The heading credits the treble to Wm. Houser, 1850, and the alto to S. M. Denson, 1911. The editors state that they searched diligently but were unable to identify the author of the tune in the older books examined.

333.title: Family Circle
333.firstLine: Come, thou fount of ev'ry blessing, Tune my heart to sing thy grace;

harmonizationAttribution.credit: Rev. R. E. Brown; S. M. Denson

333.historicalNote: The heading credits the chorus to Rev. R. E. Brown and B. F. White, 1850, and the alto to S. M. Denson, 1911. The historical note identifies B. F. White as author of the tune and gives an extended account of his work on The Sacred Harp.

334.title: O Come Away
334.firstLine: O come, come away, From labour now reposing,
334.scriptureReference: “And be not drunk with wine wherein is excess.”—Eph. 5:18
334.historicalNote: The tune was first published in The Sacred Harp by B. F. White in 1850. It is described as one of the temperance songs composed for a temperance association called the Sons of Temperance.

335.title: Return Again
335.firstLine: Saviour visit thy plantation, Grant us, Lord, a gracious rain!
335.scriptureReference: “Wilt thou not revive us again that the people may rejoice in thee?”—Ps. 85:6
335.historicalNote: The heading says “Arr. by Wm. L. Williams, 1851.” The original title of the hymn was “Prayer For Revival,” and it appeared in Olney's collection. The note also gives biographical information on Rev. William Williams.

336.title: Eternal Home
336.firstLine: Our God, our help in ages past, Our hope for years to come,
336.scriptureReference: “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations: from everlasting to everlasting thou art God.”—Ps. 90:1
336.historicalNote: The heading states that the words were arranged by J. S. James. The note says the tune was composed by S. M. Denson for the fifth edition of The Sacred Harp in 1911.

337.title: Mercy's Free
337.firstLine: What's this that in my soul is rising? Is it grace? Is it grace?
337.scriptureReference: “According to his mercy, he saved us.”—Titus 3:5
337.historicalNote: The note states that both the tune and words were credited to Breedlove in The Sacred Harp. Breedlove was a member of the Southern Musical Convention and assisted with additions to The Sacred Harp; the editors report conflicting traditions concerning when and where he died.

338.title: Sawyers Exit
338.firstLine: How bright is the day when the Christian, Receives the sweet message to come,
338.scriptureReference: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”—116 Ps. 15
338.historicalNote: The words were composed by Rev. S. B. Sawyer on the day of his death, with a request that they be published. The air is described as an old American national melody whose secular form was called “Old Rozen the Bow.” Prof. John Massengale applied Sawyer's words to the melody.

339.title: When I Am Gone
339.firstLine: Shed not a tear o'er your friend's early bier, When I am gone, When I am gone;
339.historicalNote: The note identifies Mr. Turner as both author and composer and says little was known about him beyond his membership in the Southern Musical Convention and the Chattahoochee organization; the printed note itself ends incompletely at “Chattahoo-”.

340.title: Odem
340.firstLine: Wonderful things of men are said, When they have passed away;
340.historicalNote: Thomas J. Denson composed the music and named the tune for his friend Lonnie P. Odem, who rearranged the words. The song first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision.
340.copyrightNotice: Copyrighted by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

341.title: The Lone Pilgrim
341.firstLine: I came to the place where the lone pilgrim lay,
341.scriptureReference: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also that sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.”—1 Thess. 4:14
341.historicalNote: The words and tune were composed by Major B. F. White at the grave of a friend who had once lived in Georgia, gone West, and died. The note says White wrote both words and music while visiting the grave and describes the hymn as expressing his grief for a departed friend and former companion.

342.title: The Old-Fashioned Bible
342.firstLine: How painfully pleasing the fond recollection Of youthful connections and innocent joy;
342.scriptureReference: “And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel.”—Deut. 4:44

343.title: Happy Home
343.firstLine: O yes, my Saviour I will trust; Oh, what a happy time, when the Christians all get home,
343.historicalNote: J. P. Reese composed the tune in 1859 for the second appendix of The Sacred Harp and arranged the words at the same time he made the tune.

344.title: South Union
344.firstLine: Hosanna to Jesus! I'm fill'd with his praises, Come, O my dear brethren, and help me to sing!
344.scriptureReference: “I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being.”—Ps. 146:2
344.historicalNote: The words are cited from Mercer's Cluster, page 231, third edition revised 1823, and also appear in Zion's Songster by Mason, 1832, page 102. The author of the hymn is not given. The editors were unable to identify the author of the tune; it was placed in The Sacred Harp in 1850 and is described as probably one of the old American tunes.

345t.title: Jesus Is My Friend
345t.firstLine: Come life, come death, come, then, what will, Jesus is my friend,
345t.scriptureReference: “Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you.”—St. John 15:14
345t.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

345b.title: I'm On My Journey Home
345b.firstLine: O who will come and go with me, I am on my journey home,
345b.scriptureReference: “They went forth into the land of Canaan.”—Gen. 12:5
345b.historicalNote: The piece was composed by Miss S. Lancaster in 1859; S. M. Denson added the alto in 1911. Lancaster lived in Harris County, Georgia, at the time of composition and later moved to Texas. The same words occur in the tune Journey Home by R. F. M. Mann, page 111.

346.title: The American Star
346.firstLine: The spirits of Washington, Warren, Montgomery, Look down from the clouds with bright aspect serene,
346.historicalNote: D. P. White, a son of B. F. White, is described as a lifelong Sacred Harp singer and composer who taught music in Alabama and Texas for many years. The note lists several of his other tunes in the volume.

347.title: The Blessed Bible
347.firstLine: How painfully pleasing the fond recollection, Of youthful connection and innocent joy,
347.scriptureReference: “These are the testimonies, and the statutes, and the judgments, which Moses spake unto the children of Israel.”—Deut. 4:45
347.historicalNote: The note states that the tune was composed by William L. Williams of Alabama.

348.title: Fleeting Days
348.firstLine: Time! what an empty vapor 'tis! Our days, how swift they are—
348.scriptureReference: “He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down.”—Job 14:2
348.historicalNote: Henry G. Mann composed the tune in 1869, and it was first published in The Sacred Harp. The words were arranged at the same time to suit the tune. The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

349.title: A Cross for Me
349.firstLine: Must Jesus bear the cross alone, And all the world go free?
349.historicalNote: The note describes this as one of the most popular songs in the book and says many considered it the best contribution made by O. A. Parris. Other tunes by Parris are referenced elsewhere in the volume.
349.copyrightNotice: Copyrighted, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

350.title: The Red Sea Anthem
350.firstLine: The Lord spoke unto Moses, saying, Sanctify unto me all the first born.
350.scriptureReference: “And the Lord spake unto Moses face to face.”—Exodus 33:11
350.historicalNote: The heading describes the anthem as “Original.” The note states that B. F. White composed it about 1850 for the first appendix of The Sacred Harp of White & King.

354.title: Happy Land
354.firstLine: There is a happy land, far, far away,
354.scriptureReference: “Then shall every man have the praise of God.”—1 Cor. 4:5
354.historicalNote: The note states that Leonard P. Breedlove is thought to have made changes in the treble and rearranged the chorus. The air of “Happy Land” is said to have come from the Hindoos and to have been sung widely wherever missionaries traveled.

355.title: Anthem on the Saviour
355.firstLine: My friends come listen a while And I will tell you a story About our loving Saviour;
355.scriptureReference: Matthew 1:23; Isaiah 9:6; Luke 20:17; John 1:11; and other passages
355.historicalNote: The anthem is supposed to have been composed by Prof. B. F. White in 1859, although the note allows that it may have been composed earlier. It was placed in The Sacred Harp in 1859. The words are stated to be predicated on several Biblical passages.

358.title: Murillo's Lesson
358.firstLine: As down a lone valley with cedars o'erspread, From wars dread confusion I pensively strayed,
358.scriptureReference: “The valleys are spread forth as gardens by the river's side, the trees the Lord hath planted, cedar trees beside the waters.”—Num. 24:6
358.historicalNote: The note explicitly states that it is not known who composed the music.

359.title: The Bride's Farewell
359.firstLine: Farewell, mother, tears are beaming Down thy pale and tender cheek;
359.scriptureReference: “And they lifted up their voice, and wept again: but Ruth clave unto her.”—Ruth 1:14
359.historicalNote: The heading says “Arranged 1869 by H. S. Rees” and also credits H. S. Rees, 1869. The note states that the tune as printed was composed by Rees in 1869 specifically for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp and had not been found in another book except later Sacred Harp revisions.

360.title: The Royal Band
360.firstLine: Hosanna to Jesus, my soul's fill'd with praises, Come, O my dear brethren, and help me to sing;
360.scriptureReference: “Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.”—Matt. 21:9
360.historicalNote: Little was known of W. T. Power. He was a member of the Southern Musical Convention and the Chattahoochee Singing Convention. The note says this was the only tune and hymn by him that the editors had been able to ascertain.

361.title: Loving Jesus
361.firstLine: Here's my heart, my loving Jesus, Here's my heart, my loving Jesus,
361.scriptureReference: “My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways.”—Prov. 23:26
361.historicalNote: The heading credits “White & Searcy, 1850.” The prose beneath the tune, however, calls B. F. White the author of the tune. That difference is retained rather than reconciled.

362.title: Norwich
362.firstLine: Oh the delights, the heav'nly joys, The glories of the place
362.scriptureReference: “These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.”—John 15:11
362.historicalNote: Norwich is credited in The Sacred Harp to D. P. White. The outlines of the tune are said to be traceable to early nineteenth-century books, but D. P. White rearranged and remodeled it for the third appendix in 1869.

365.title: Southwell
365.firstLine: 'Tis finish'd, 'tis finish'd, 'tis finish'd, 'tis finish'd, The Redeemer said,
365.scriptureReference: “Jesus said, It is finished: and he bowed his head and gave up the ghost.”—John 19:30
365.historicalNote: The poetry was composed by Samuel Stennett in 1778. After considerable searching, the editors state that they were unable to identify the author of the tune Southwell.

367.title: Consolation
367.firstLine: Awake dear brother, sister, friend, Get ready for the call;
367.historicalNote: The note explicitly states that both words and music were written by Mrs. Annie Denson Aaron, oldest daughter of Thomas J. and Amanda Burdette Denson. She is described as an excellent treble singer.
367.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

368.title: Draketown
368.firstLine: Alas and did my Savior bleed? And did my Sov'reign die?
368.historicalNote: Howard Denson, younger son of Thomas J. and Amanda Burdette Denson, wrote the song in 1935. He is described as an outstanding bass singer and good leader. See page 373.
368.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

369.title: Send a Blessing
369.firstLine: O, tell me no more of this world's vain store, The time for such trifles with me now is o'er.

musicAttribution.credit: B. F. White and L. L. Ledbetter

369.scriptureReference: “Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.”—John 1:51
369.historicalNote: The hymn is taken from Gambold's works of 1748 and originally contained fourteen three-line stanzas. The note gives biographical information on John Gambold, a Moravian or United Brethren bishop who died in 1771.

370.title: Monroe
370.firstLine: Jesus, I my cross have taken, All to leave and follow thee;
370.scriptureReference: “Let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me.”—Matt. 16:24
370.historicalNote: The hymn was composed in 1832 by Henry Francis Lyte under the title “Lo, we have left all and followed thee.” The full hymn is said to contain six double stanzas. W. S. Turner is identified as author of the tune; he was a Methodist minister and died in 1891.

371.title: Heavenly Dove
371.firstLine: Come, Holy Spirit, heav'nly Dove, With all Thy quick'ning pow'rs;
371.scriptureReference: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it abode upon him.”—John 1:32

372.title: Lakeland
372.firstLine: There is a fountain filled with blood, Drawn from Immanuel's veins;
372.historicalNote: The tune was composed by W. T. (Pansy) Mitchell. He was a nephew of Amanda Burdette Denson and, after his parents died during his infancy, was reared in the Thomas J. Denson home.
372.copyrightNotice: Copyrighted, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

373.title: Homeward Bound
373.firstLine: The Lord is leading me today, His love shines all around;
373.historicalNote: The note states that this was Howard Denson's first composition in dispersed harmony. He wrote it and Draketown, page 368, for the 1936 Denson Revision. His friend O. A. Parris wrote the words.
373.copyrightNotice: Copyrighted, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

374.title: Oh, Sing with Me!
374.firstLine: Oh! sing with me of social spheres, Where breathes in kindness mutual love;
374.scriptureReference: “Serve the Lord with gladness: come before his presence with singing.”—100 Ps. 2
374.historicalNote: Miss P. R. Lancaster composed the tune in 1859 for the second appendix of The Sacred Harp. She was then living in Harris County, Georgia, later moved to Texas, and had been instructed in music by J. P. Rees and B. F. White. S. M. Denson composed the alto in 1911.

375.title: Love the Lord
375.firstLine: Alas and did my Saviour bleed, And did my sov'reign die,
375.scriptureReference: “Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love.”—Jer. 31:3
375.historicalNote: J. P. Rees composed Love the Lord for the second appendix of The Sacred Harp in 1859.

376.title: Help Me to Sing
376.firstLine: Ye souls who are bound unto Canaan, Come join in and help me to sing
376.scriptureReference: “Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him.”—Ps. 105:2
376.historicalNote: B. F. White composed the tune for the second appendix of The Sacred Harp in 1859. The note states that the other musical parts, including the hymn, remain as printed in 1859, with the alto added by S. M. Denson in 1911.

377.title: Eternal Praise
377.firstLine: From all that dwell below the skies, Let the Creator's praise arise;
377.historicalNote: The music was written by Oren A. Parris and first published in the 1936 Denson Revision. He is described as one of the best-informed singers, teachers, and writers in the Deep South in both modern and dispersed harmony. See page 481.
377.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

378t.title: Heavenly Port
378t.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand, And cast a wishful eye,
378t.scriptureReference: “Thine eyes shall behold the land that is very far off.”—Isa. 33:17
378t.historicalNote: The tune was composed by Elder Edmund Dumas in 1859 for the second appendix of The Sacred Harp. Dumas is described as a Primitive Baptist minister and musician of considerable note who died and was buried at Forsyth, Monroe County, Georgia.

378b.title: Never Turn Back
378b.firstLine: When to that blessed world I rise, I'll never turn back any more;

harmonizationAttribution.credit: J. P. Reese and Miss F. E. Parkerson; S. M. Denson

378b.scriptureReference: “Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way.”—Psa. 44:18
378b.historicalNote: The heading explicitly says “Arr for the Organ, by J. P. Reese and Miss F. E. Parkerson, 1859,” with the alto by S. M. Denson, 1911. No original composer is identified on the page.

379.title: Span of Life
379.firstLine: My span of life will soon be gone, The passing moments say:
379.scriptureReference: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.”—Ps. 90:12
379.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” The note refers to the history of S. M. Brown under Man's Redemption elsewhere in the volume.

380.title: Lawrenceburg
380.firstLine: Oh, if my Lord should come and meet, My soul would stretch her wings in haste,
380.historicalNote: Thomas J. Denson composed the tune in 1935 for the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 426.
380.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

381.title: Sing On
381.firstLine: Farewell my friends weep not for me, I'm going home to God;
381.copyrightNotice: Copyright by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

382.title: Coston
382.firstLine: Dear friends, farewell I do you tell, Since you and I must part;
382.historicalNote: The music was written by Thomas J. Denson and named for his friend W. T. Coston of Fort Worth, Texas. See page 426 for additional information.
382.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

383.title: Eternal Day
383.firstLine: O what of all my sufferings here, if, Lord, thou count me meet
383.scriptureReference: “He became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him.”—Heb. 5:9
383.historicalNote: The heading describes the music as original and credits J. P. Rees, 1859, with S. M. Denson's alto added in 1911.

384.title: Panting for Heaven
384.firstLine: Oh, when will the period appear, When I shall unite in your song?
384.scriptureReference: “Man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.”—Lam. 3:26
384.historicalNote: S. M. Brown composed the tune in 1869 for the second appendix to The Sacred Harp. The note says he lived in Haralson County, Georgia, at the time of his death, about twenty years or more before the note was written.

385t.title: Fight On.
385t.firstLine: Fight on my soul 'till death Shall bring thee to thy God,
385t.scriptureReference: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.”—2 Tim. 4:7
385t.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

385b.title: Can I Leave You?
385b.firstLine: Yes, my native land, I love thee, All thy scenes I love them well;
385b.historicalNote: The heading says “Arr. by John Rees 1852” and separately credits the alto to S. M. Denson, 1911.

386.title: Christ Our Song
386.firstLine: Awake my heart, arise my tongue, Prepare a tuneful voice;
386.historicalNote: The heading says “arr. by T. B. McG.” The note states that the song was written by Thomas B. McGraw in 1935 for the 1936 Denson Revision and refers to page 558 for additional information.
386.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

387.title: Penick
387.firstLine: While trav'ling thro' the world below, Where sore afflictions come,
387.historicalNote: The heading credits M. Sykes of Montgomery County, Georgia, 1857. The note says little was known about him; he had been active in the Southern Musical Convention in the 1850s. The tune was written in honor of Prof. S. R. Penick, and the editors note a claim that Penick himself wrote the words.

388.title: The Happy Sailor
388.firstLine: Come tell of your ship and what is her name, Oh, tell me, happy Sailor!

harmonizationAttribution.credit: B. F. White; S. M. Denson

388.scriptureReference: “Having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breast plate of righteousness.”—Eph. 6:14
388.historicalNote: B. F. White rearranged the tune for the second appendix of The Sacred Harp in 1859; S. M. Denson added the alto in 1911. The editors were unable to identify the author of the words of the first verse. C. J. Griggs of Atlanta composed the second and third verses in 1911.

389.title: Fredericksburg
389.firstLine: I need God's blessings while I live, And His undying love;
389.historicalNote: Oscar H. Frederick composed the tune. He attended a singing school taught by Thomas J. Denson and became a good singer and successful teacher of Sacred Harp music.
389.copyrightNotice: Copyright, 1936, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc.

390.title: New Prospect
390.firstLine: O land of rest for thee I sigh: When will the moment come
390.scriptureReference: “Yes, saith the Spirit, that they rest from their labors.”—Rev. 14:13
390.historicalNote: W. S. Turner was a son of J. R. Turner and a Methodist minister. Father and son composed and prepared many tunes with the intention of publishing a note and song book, but both died before it was completed and the manuscript was lost or burned.

391.title: Sounding Joy
391.firstLine: Behold the morning sun, Begins his glorious way,
391.scriptureReference: “Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun.”—Eccl. 11:7
391.historicalNote: B. F. White is identified as author of the tune. The note describes him as one of the compilers of The Sacred Harp in 1844 and as a participant in the appendices of 1850, 1859, and 1869.

392.title: Manchester
392.firstLine: There is a land of pure delight, Where saints immortal reign;
392.historicalNote: Paine Denson composed the tune in 1935 for the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 524.
392.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

393.title: Fairview
393.firstLine: Religion is the chief concern, Of mortals here below;
393.historicalNote: Thomas J. Denson composed the song, which first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 426 for additional information.
393.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

394.title: The Messiah's Praise
394.firstLine: My heart and voice I raise To spread Messiah's praise,

musicAttribution.credit: R. F. M. Mann and James A. Sparks

394.scriptureReference: “Every man have praise of God.”—1 Cor. 4:5
394.historicalNote: The tune was composed by R. F. M. Mann and James A. Sparks. The note refers to other sketches of Mann and states that little was known of James A. Sparks, who had reportedly been dead for many years.

395.title: New Bethel
395.firstLine: O for a thousand tongues to sing My great Redeemer's praise;
395.historicalNote: The tune was composed by L. A. McGraw for the 1936 Denson Revision. See footnote on page 284.
395.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

396.title: Notes Almost Divine
396.firstLine: Oh, could I speak the matchless worth, Oh, could I sound the glories forth,
396.historicalNote: For additional information on Paine Denson, composer of the tune, the note refers to the footnote on page 524.
396.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

397.title: The Fountain
397.firstLine: There is a fountain filled with blood, Drawn from Immanuel's veins;
397.historicalNote: The tune was composed by Thomas J. Denson for the 1936 Denson Revision. See pages 426 and 427.
397.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

398.title: The Dying Boy
398.firstLine: I'm dying, mother, dying now, please raise my aching head,
398.scriptureReference: “Jesus saw her weeping, and was troubled.”—John 11:33

399t.title: The Dying Friend
399t.firstLine: Young people hear me as your friend, Whose days on earth are at an end;
399t.historicalNote: Lee Wells of Jasper, Alabama, composed the tune. He is described as a good singer, smooth leader, and popular among his singing friends, and was trained by Thomas J. Denson.
399t.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

399b.title: Happy Christian
399b.firstLine: Oh, how happy are they, Who their Savior obey,
399b.historicalNote: B. E. Cunningham composed the tune for the 1936 Denson Revision. He is described as one of the leading singers and supporters of Sacred Harp music in northwestern Alabama.
399b.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

400.title: Struggle On
400.firstLine: Our praying time will soon be o'er, Hallelujah, We'll join with those who've gone before, Hallelujah.
400.scriptureReference: “Hear my cry, O God; attend unto my prayer.”—Ps. 61:1
400.historicalNote: The note explicitly identifies this as another of H. S. Rees's compositions, both words and music. It is described as a favorite melody often sung in musical conventions.

401.title: Cuba
401.firstLine: Go, preachers, and tell it to the world, Go, preachers, and tell it to the world,

musicAttribution.credit: J. H. Bolen and H. S. Reese

401.scriptureReference: “Go ye therefore and teach all nations.”—Matt. 28:19

402.title: Protection
402.firstLine: The Lord my pasture shall prepare, And feed me with a shepherd's care;
402.scriptureReference: “The Lord is my Shepherd I shall not want.”—Psa. 23:1
402.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” The note says the hymn was composed by Addison and originally had four verses; it is based on the 23rd Psalm and originally titled “Trust in the Supreme Being.” Protection is also cited in Lute of Zion, page 187, and the words in several other books.

403.title: Heavenly Rest
403.firstLine: How happy are the souls above, From sin and sorrow free;
403.scriptureReference: “Then shall ye also appear with him in glory.”—Col. 3:4
403.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

404.title: Youth Will Soon Be Gone
404.firstLine: Youth like the spring, will soon be gone, By fleeting Time or conqu'ring Death,
404.scriptureReference: “From the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth.”—Ps. 110:3
404.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

405.title: The Marcellas
405.firstLine: Children of the heavenly King, As we journey sweetly sing;
405.scriptureReference: “To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ forever.”—Rom. 16:27
405.historicalNote: The hymn was first published in 1742 and originally had twelve stanzas. The note gives brief biographical information on John Cennick but does not identify the composer of the tune.

406.title: New Harmony
406.firstLine: I want to live a Christian here, I want to die a shouting,
406.scriptureReference: “For in him we live, and move, and have our being.”—Acts 17:28
406.historicalNote: The heading says “Arranged by Miss M. L. A. Lancaster, 1859.” The note states that additional verses were added in 1911, while the first was retained as it had appeared in The Sacred Harp by Major White and was the final verse of the original hymn.

407.title: Charlton
407.firstLine: My span of life will soon be done, The passing moments say,
407.scriptureReference: “For I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.”—Phil. 4:11
407.historicalNote: The heading credits L. P. Breedlove, 1859. The note below instead says “L. B. Breedlove composed the above tune in 1859,” so the conflicting middle initial is retained rather than reconciled.

408.title: Weeping Mary
408.firstLine: They crucified the Saviour, They crucified the Saviour,
408.scriptureReference: “Saying, She goeth unto the grave to weep there.”—St. John 11:31

409.title: Promised Day
409.firstLine: How long dear Saviour, Oh, how long shall this bright hour delay?
409.scriptureReference: “I say unto you, hereafter ye shall see heaven open.”—John 1:51
409.historicalNote: The heading credits L. M. Ranford, 1859. The biographical note, however, says Ranford composed the tune in 1856 while living in Harris County, Georgia; the conflicting date is preserved here.

410t.title: The Dying Californian
410t.firstLine: Lay up nearer, brother, nearer, For my limbs are growing cold;
410t.historicalNote: The heading states “Re-arr. and Alto added by Howard Denson, 1935.” No printed key designation is given.

410b.title: Mutual Love
410b.firstLine: O when shall I see Jesus, And reign with Him above?
410b.historicalNote: The heading credits Wm. Walker, 1835, and says “Re-arr. by Howard Denson, 1935.” The note explicitly states that William Walker composed the tune and Howard Denson rearranged it for the 1936 Denson Revision.

411.title: Morning Prayer
411.firstLine: Come, let us raise our voices high, And form a sacred song,
411.historicalNote: Thomas J. Denson wrote the tune for the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 426.
411.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

412.title: New Hosanna
412.firstLine: Wake, O my soul, and hail the morn, For unto us a Saviour's born;
412.scriptureReference: “Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord, Hosanna in the highest.”—Matt. 21:9
412.historicalNote: The heading cites J. Dobell's New Selection, 1806. The tune was placed in the second appendix to The Sacred Harp in 1859. The note also cites The Timbrel of Zion, page 319, and Christian Harmony by William Walker, page 214.

413.title: The Loved Ones
413.firstLine: Be kind to thy father, for when thou wert young, Who loved thee so fondly as he?
413.scriptureReference: “A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish man despiseth his mother.”—Prov. 15:20

414.title: Parting Friend
414.firstLine: The time must come when we must part, When we must say Farewell?

harmonizationAttribution.credit: J. C. Graham; S. M. Denson

414.historicalNote: The heading explicitly says “Arr. by J. C. Graham, 1859,” with alto by S. M. Denson, 1911; no original composer is identified.

415.title: Endless Praise
415.firstLine: When we've been there ten thousand years, Bright shining as the sun;
415.historicalNote: J. D. (Dee) Wall composed the tune for the 1936 Denson Revision. He attended singing schools taught by Seaborn M. and Thomas J. Denson and was described as a good singer and successful Sacred Harp teacher.
415.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

416.title: The Christian's Nightly Song
416.firstLine: I'll sing my Saviour's grace, And his sweet name I'll praise,
416.scriptureReference: “To the praise of the glory of his grace.”—Eph. 1:6
416.historicalNote: E. T. Pound is described as one of Georgia's best-known music teachers and composers. The note identifies The Loved Ones and The Christian's Nightly Song as his two Sacred Harp tunes and says he taught singing schools in Georgia for more than fifty years.

417.title: Weeping Pilgrim
417.firstLine: You may tell them father when you see them—I'm a poor mourning Pilgrim, I'm bound for Canaan's land.
417.scriptureReference: “And the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying.”—Isa. 5:19
417.historicalNote: The note identifies J. P. Rees as author of the tune and gives biographical information: born in Jasper County, Georgia, in 1828; long resident of Coweta County; musician and convention leader; died in 1900 and buried at Newnan, Georgia.

418.title: Rees
418.firstLine: There is a house not made with hands, Eternal and on high;
418.scriptureReference: “An house not made with hands.”—2 Cor. 5:1
418.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” Elder Edward Dumas composed it in 1859 for J. P. Rees, one of his musical brethren.

419.title: Melancholy Day
419.firstLine: Death, 'tis a melancholy day, To those who have no God,
419.scriptureReference: “The fool hath said in his heart, there is no God.”—Ps. 14:1
419.historicalNote: The note identifies Rev. H. S. Rees as author of the music and gives biographical information, including that his first Sacred Harp tune was Traveling Pilgrim, page 278.

420.title: Bishop
420.firstLine: Our Father's gone to that bright land, He dwells with Christ the King;
420.historicalNote: The tune first appeared in the 1936 Denson Revision. Thomas B. McGraw wrote the music and named it for his wife, who wrote the words. See page 558.
420.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

421.title: Sweet Morning
421.firstLine: The happy day will soon appear, And we'll all shout together in that morning.

harmonizationAttribution.credit: H. S. Rees; S. M. Denson

421.scriptureReference: “And let him hear the cry in the morning, and the shouting at noon-tide.”—Jer. 20:16
421.historicalNote: The heading credits H. S. Rees as arranger and S. M. Denson with the alto, 1911. The prose below instead calls Rev. H. S. Rees the author of the music. Rees was born in Jasper County, Georgia, in 1828 and was a twin brother of J. P. Rees; his first Sacred Harp tune was Traveling Pilgrim.

422.title: Burdette
422.firstLine: Oh, for a heart to praise my God, A heart from sin set free,
422.scriptureReference: “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.”—Eph. 1:7
422.historicalNote: Whit Denson named the tune Burdette in honor of his grandparents, Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Burdette. The note identifies him as a fine singer, director of music, and teacher of singing schools.

423.title: Grantville
423.firstLine: Should earth against my soul engage, And fiery darts be hurled.
423.scriptureReference: “That we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.”—Heb. 4:16
423.historicalNote: The note identifies J. P. Reese as author of the tune and gives biographical information: born in Jasper County, Georgia, in 1828; longtime resident of Coweta County; music leader and convention president; died in 1900 and buried at Newnan, Georgia.

424.title: Sweet Union
424.firstLine: Awake my soul in joyful lays, Oh, Glory Hallelujah, And sing thy great Redeemer's praise.
424.historicalNote: The note identifies J. P. Reese as author of the tune and gives a brief account of his musical and convention work. The tune concludes on page 425.

425.title: Golden Streets
425.firstLine: I am on my journey home, I am on my journey home,
425.historicalNote: J. L. Pickard composed the tune in 1859 for the second appendix of The Sacred Harp. The note states that nothing is known of him.

426t.title: Kelley
426t.firstLine: My Christian friends to whom I speak, I have a crown in view;
426t.scriptureReference: “For ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another.”—1 Thess. 4:9
426t.historicalNote: Mrs. Amanda Denson is described as a fine singer and leader who participated in singing conventions and teaching. Her maiden name was Burdette. The note states that she died at Helicon, Alabama, in the fall of 1910.

426b.title: Jasper
426b.firstLine: Great God let all thy tuneful pow'r Awake and sing thy praise.
426b.scriptureReference: “I will sing unto the Lord as long as I live.”—Ps. 104:33
426b.historicalNote: The heading specifically says “Words rearranged by T. J. Denson, 1907.” The tune continues onto page 427, where a long biographical note describes Thomas J. Denson's work as a singer, teacher, composer, and member of the Denson musical family.

428.title: World Unknown
428.firstLine: And am I born to die, To lay this body down,
428.scriptureReference: If a man die, shall he live again.—Job 14:14
428.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” The note identifies Rev. H. S. Reese as author of the music and notes that he was born in Jasper County, Georgia, in 1828 and was a twin brother of J. P. Reese.

429.title: Christian's Delight
429.firstLine: Peace, troubled soul, thou need not fear, Jesus says he will be with us to the end.
429.scriptureReference: “He will not forsake thee, neither destroy thee.”—Deut. 4:31
429.historicalNote: The hymn was first published in the author's hymn book under “Grace Faith and Repentance” and was composed before the nineteenth century. The note states that it was used in 1806 by an itinerant preacher during travels through early Louisiana.

430.title: Arbacoochee
430.firstLine: Behold the love, the generous love, That holy David shows,
430.scriptureReference: Typical of Christ's love for the church.—Isa. 63:3
430.historicalNote: The words are stated to be the same as those used with Sardinia on page 296. The note says they were favorites of Wiley J. James of Tallapoosa, Georgia, an admirer of the old sacred songs.

431.title: New Bethany
431.firstLine: Ere mountains rear'd their forms sublime, Or heav'n and earth in order stood,
431.scriptureReference: “Before the mountains were, or thou formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.”—Ps. 90:2
431.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” B. F. White, Jr., author of the tune, was a son of B. F. White and was living in Atlanta in 1911. New Bethany was composed for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp.

432.title: Cheves
432.firstLine: Grace, 'tis a most delightful theme, 'Tis grace that rescues guilty man,
432.scriptureReference: “My grace is sufficient for thee.”—2 Cor. 12:9
