432.historicalNote: Oliver Bradfield composed Cheves in 1857. The words of the hymn were changed from the original so as to fit the tune. The tune was not printed until 1869. Bradfield also composed Hope, Williams, and We'll Soon Be There and was a member of the Southern Musical Convention.

433.title: McKay
433.firstLine: O the transporting, rapturous scene, That rises to my sight!
433.scriptureReference: “And he showed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and the Lamb.”—Rev. 22:1
433.historicalNote: The text consists of the second and third verses of the hymn “On Jordan's Stormy Banks I Stand.” The hymn was written by Samuel Stennett and was named “Promised Land” in Rippon's Selection. The note mentions a claim that it imitates Isaac Watts's “There is a Land of Pure Delight.”

434.title: Fillmore
434.firstLine: Great God, let all my tuneful pow'rs Awake, and sing thy mighty name;
434.scriptureReference: “I will sing unto the Lord as long as I live.”—Ps. 104:33
434.historicalNote: John P. Rees, author of the tune, was born in Jasper County, Georgia, in 1828 and died in Newnan, Georgia, in 1900. He served for years as president of the Chattahoochee Singing Convention and the Southern Musical Convention.

435.title: Sacred Rest
435.firstLine: Sweet is the day of sacred rest, No mortal care shall fill my breast;
435.historicalNote: The tune was composed by W. D. Jones in 1869. The note refers to another sketch of Jones in the volume and to the fuller history of the hymn under Devotion, page 48. The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

436.title: Morning Sun
436.firstLine: Youth, like the spring, will soon be gone, By fleeting time or conquering death;
436.scriptureReference: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh.”—Eccl. 12:1
436.historicalNote: S. M. Denson composed Morning Sun for the fifth edition of The Original Sacred Harp. The note states that the words were applied to the tune by J. S. James, that the hymn is an exhortation to the young, and that Denson was particularly fond of fugue tunes.

437.title: Sidney
437.firstLine: My Shepherd will supply my need, Jehovah is His name,
437.scriptureReference: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep.”—John 10:11
437.historicalNote: The words were arranged by H. A. Parris, a singer and writer of music residing at Helicon, Alabama. Whit Denson is identified as a son of Mr. and Mrs. S. M. Denson.

438.title: The Marriage in the Skies
438.firstLine: O ring the bells of heaven high, The marriage feast has come,
438.scriptureReference: “Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. Let us be glad and rejoice and give honor to him: for the marriage feast of the Lamb has come.”—Rev. 19:9, 7
438.historicalNote: The note identifies Mrs. Sidney Denson as author of the tune and music. She was a Burdette before marriage, had been musical since childhood, assisted her husband in teaching and convention work, and served as a leader and director of singing schools.

439.title: Jordan
439.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand, And cast a wishful eye
439.historicalNote: The note refers to the history of Samuel Stennett under Promised Land. Professor Cagle is described as an Alabama resident, lover of old sacred songs, good leader, fine singer, and well regarded among the music people.

440.title: North Salem
440.firstLine: My soul come meditate the day, And think how near it stands,
440.scriptureReference: “But truly as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, there is but a step between me and death.”—1 Sam. 20:3
440.historicalNote: Stephen Jenks of New Canaan, Connecticut, published Delights of Harmony in 1805; twenty-six tunes in that book were his compositions. The work was published by subscription. He later removed to Thompson and died there in 1856.

441.title: Raymond
441.firstLine: Hark, the glad sound! the Saviour comes, The Saviour promised long;
441.scriptureReference: “The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.”—Luke 4:18-19

442.title: New Jordan
442.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand, And cast a wishful eye,

harmonizationAttribution.credit: S. M. Denson and J. S. James

442.scriptureReference: “Thine eyes shall behold the King in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off.”—Isa. 33:17
442.historicalNote: The heading says the tune was remodeled by S. M. Denson and J. S. James on April 29, 1911. The note identifies the hymn title as “Christ's Message,” calls it Doddridge's masterpiece, and states that the complete hymn has five verses but only two are included here.

444.title: All Saints New
444.firstLine: Oh, if my Lord would come and meet, my soul should stretch her wings in haste,
444.scriptureReference: “Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his.”—Num. 23:10
444.historicalNote: Amrick Hall, author of the tune, was born at Rayham, Massachusetts, in 1785 and died in 1827. The note says All Saints New is claimed by historians as his masterpiece and describes it as difficult to render but a fine old melody. See further remarks under Devotion, page 48.

445.title: Passing Away
445.firstLine: And must I be to judgment brought, and answer in that day
445.scriptureReference: “It is appointed unto man once to die, but after this the judgment.”—Heb. 9:27
445.historicalNote: The tune as printed is credited to John A. Watson, 1872. The note cites Christian Harmony by William Walker, 1866, revised 1901, page 130.

446.title: Infinite Day
446.firstLine: There is a land of pure delight, Where saints immortal reign;
446.historicalNote: This is identified as the first composition by Ruth Denson Edwards of Cullman, Alabama, youngest daughter of Thomas J. Denson and Amanda Burdette Denson. See page 543.
446.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

447.title: Wondrous Cross
447.firstLine: When I survey the wondrous cross On which the Prince of glory died,
447.historicalNote: The music was composed in 1932 by Paine Denson. The note describes the tune and Isaac Watts's words as conveying an impressive message. See page 524.
447.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

448t.title: Consecration
448t.firstLine: There then to thee thine own I leave, mould as thy will thy passive clay;
448t.scriptureReference: “Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy acceptable unto God.”—Rom. 12:1
448t.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” The note identifies W. S. Turner as a son of J. R. Turner and a Methodist minister; his father was for many years a singing teacher and composed several tunes.

448b.title: The Grieved Soul
448b.firstLine: Come my soul and let us try, For a little season,
448b.scriptureReference: “For he doth not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men.”—Lam. 3:33
448b.historicalNote: The editors state that they were unable to obtain reliable biographical information about Miss M. A. Hendon, composer of the tune, beyond that she lived for a long time in Harris County, Georgia.

449.title: Fatherland
449.firstLine: There is a place where my hopes are stay'd, My heart and my treasures are there;
449.scriptureReference: “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”—Matt. 6:21
449.historicalNote: The editors state that they found no trace in the books consulted concerning the authorship of either the tune or words beyond the credit printed on the page.

450.title: Elder
450.firstLine: Gently glides the stream of life, Oft along the flow'ry vale,
450.scriptureReference: “But the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”—2 Cor. 4:18
450.historicalNote: The tune was composed for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp. The note refers to the sketch of M. Mark Wynn under Doddridge and states that the words were rearranged by the author to suit the tune when it was first published in 1869.

451.title: Mary's Grief and Joy
451.firstLine: Mary to her Saviour's tomb Hasted at the early dawn;
451.scriptureReference: “Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him.”—Mark 16:1
451.historicalNote: Major B. F. White arranged the tune for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp in 1869. The editors state that they were unable to identify the original composer. The hymn was composed by John Newton.

452.title: Martin
452.firstLine: Jesus, Lover of my soul, Let me to Thy bosom fly;
452.historicalNote: The note identifies the hymn as “Jesus, Lover of My Soul” and discusses its prominence among Charles Wesley's hymns.

453.title: Holly Springs
453.firstLine: There is a house not made with hands, Eternal and on high;
453.historicalNote: The tune is described as one of H. N. McGraw's first compositions and was written for the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 492 for additional information.
453.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

454.title: The Better Land
454.firstLine: The road to glory seems so long, And sorrows often take my song;
454.copyrightNotice: Copyright by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

455.title: Soar Away
455.firstLine: I want a sober mind, An all sustaining eye, To see my God above, And to the heavens fly.
455.historicalNote: The song is described as a general favorite. It was written by A. Marcus Cagle for the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 507.
455.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

456.title: Sacred Mount
456.firstLine: Sing, O ye ransomed of the Lord, your great Redeemer sing.
456.historicalNote: The heading also says “Arr by A. M. C.” The note states that A. Marcus Cagle composed the song in 1935 for the 1936 Denson Revision. See page 507.
456.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

457.title: Wayfaring Stranger
457.firstLine: I am a poor wayfaring stranger, While journeying thru this world of woe,
457.historicalNote: The note describes this as a well-known southern folk song that had not appeared in The Sacred Harp before the 1936 Denson Revision. For that edition, both the music and words were rearranged by John M. Dye of Birmingham, Alabama.
457.copyrightNotice: Copyright, by Sacred Harp Publishing Co., Inc., 1936

458.title: Friendship
458.firstLine: Mercy, O thou son of David, Thus poor blind Bartimeus prayed;
458.scriptureReference: “Thou son of David, have mercy on me.”—Mark 10:48
458.historicalNote: The editors state that they were unable to obtain reliable information about E. F. Williams beyond his association at one time with the Southern Musical Convention and the Chattahoochee Singing Convention.

459.title: Tolling Bell
459.firstLine: Shed not a tear o'er your friend's early bier, When I am gone, When I am gone;
459.historicalNote: R. F. M. Mann wrote the tune for the fourth edition of The Sacred Harp in memory of Misses M. H. White and E. A. Mann. The words are those associated with When I Am Gone, page 339, and the note states that M. H. Turner is supposed to have composed them in 1859.

460.title: Sardis
460.firstLine: Come on, my fellow pilgrims, come, And let us all be hastening home,
460.scriptureReference: “There shall be no more death, neither sorrow, ... for the former things have passed away.”—Rev. 21:4
460.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.”

461.title: Farewell
461.firstLine: Farewell, my dear brethren, the time is at hand, Our sev'ral engagements now call us away;
461.historicalNote: The heading describes the tune as “Original.” The words were selected from Zions Songster, 1832. W. D. Jones was living in Carroll County, Georgia, in April 1911 and had been a member of the Chattahoochee Singing Convention for more than forty years.

462.title: Faith and Hope
462.firstLine: What shall I do, shall I lie down and sink in deep despair? Will He forever wear a frown nor hear my feeble prayer?
462.historicalNote: The heading also says “Arr. by A. M. Cagle.” Alfred Marcus Cagle is identified as composer of the tune and an authority on dispersed harmony. He died at Villa Rica, Georgia, December 19, 1968.
462.copyrightNotice: Copyright, 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company

463.title: Our Humble Faith
463.firstLine: Lord, how divine thy comforts are, How heav'nly is the place,
463.historicalNote: The heading also says “Arr. by G. S. Doss.” The page refers to the footnote on page 503 for additional information.
463.copyrightNotice: © 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, Inc.

464.title: Crown Him
464.firstLine: Crown Him with many crowns, The Lamb upon His throne,
464.historicalNote: The page refers to the footnote on page 558 for additional information.
464.copyrightNotice: © 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, Inc.

465.title: Where There's No Trouble and Sorrow
465.firstLine: I have my troubles here below As the narrow way I follow, But there's a land of peace and rest, Where there's no trouble and sorrow.
465.historicalNote: Doris W. DeLong is identified as composer of the tune, living in Roswell, Georgia, and as a good singer and leader of Sacred Harp music.
465.copyrightNotice: © 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, Inc.

466.title: Admonition
466.firstLine: Come, ye that love the Lord, And let your joys be known,
466.historicalNote: Thomas Jackson Denson, composer of the tune, died September 14, 1935, and was buried in Fairview Cemetery near Double Springs, Winston County, Alabama. See page 426.
466.copyrightNotice: © 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, Inc.

467.title: Lisbon
467.firstLine: Welcome sweet day of rest, That saw the Lord arise;
467.historicalNote: The heading states “Theme by Read” and “Alto by A. M. Cagle 1960.”

468.title: Seaborn
468.firstLine: When Gabriel gives the trumpets blast, Declares that time shall be no more,
468.historicalNote: The tune continues through page 469. The page refers to the footnote on page 477.
468.copyrightNotice: Copyright, 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company

470.title: The Mercy Seat
470.firstLine: From ev'ry stormy wind that blows, From ev'ry swelling tide of woes,
470.historicalNote: The page refers to the footnote on page 547.
470.copyrightNotice: © 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, Inc.

471.title: The Saviour's Name
471.firstLine: There is a name I love to hear, I love to sing its worth;
471.copyrightNotice: 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, Inc.

472.title: Macedonia
472.firstLine: Salvation, O, melodious sound, To wretched dying men,
472.historicalNote: T. J. Entrekin of Tifton, Georgia, composed the song. He is described as related to the McGraw family and a lifelong supporter of Sacred Harp music. The words are by Doddridge.
472.copyrightNotice: © 1960, by The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, Inc.

473.title: Carmarthen
473.firstLine: Rejoice! the Lord is King! Your Lord and King adore,

572.title: The Lamb of God
572.firstLine: In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness, crying with a loud voice, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sins of the world.”
572.historicalNote: The heading says “Arr. by Rev. P. M.” Reverend Priestley Miller (1905–1969), pastor of Harpeth Presbyterian Church in Nashville, Tennessee, composed the tune. He founded the Harpeth Valley Sacred Harp Singing Association and published and edited the Harpeth Valley Sacred Harp News.
